f\text{ is defined on a neighborhood of }x\in E
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: H_s'(x)\iff H_w'(x)\iff F'(x),\qquad d_H^s f(x;\cdot)=d_H^w f(x;\cdot)=Df(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hierarchy of Fréchet, weak Hadamard, strong Hadamard, and Gâteaux differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implications among differentiability notions on normed spaces and the stated reflexive-Banach-space equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a normed vector space and let \(f:V(x)\to\mathbb R\) be defined on a neighborhood of \(x\in E\). Fréchet differentiability at \(x\) implies weak Hadamard differentiability, and \(d_H^w f(x;v)=L(x)v\) for every \(v\in E\). Weak Hadamard differentiability implies strong Hadamard differentiability, which implies Gâteaux differentiability. If \(E\) is a reflexive Banach space, weak Hadamard differentiability at \(x\) is equivalent to Fréchet differentiability at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fréchet differentiability implies weak Hadamard differentiability, which implies strong Hadamard differentiability, which implies Gâteaux differentiability. On a reflexive Banach space, weak Hadamard and Fréchet differentiability are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: E\text{ is a normed vector space}
f:V(x)\to\mathbb R\text{ is defined on a neighborhood of }x\in E
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F'(x)\Rightarrow H_w'(x)\Rightarrow H_s'(x)\Rightarrow G'(x),\qquad d_H^w f(x;v)=L(x)v;\qquad E\text{ reflexive Banach}\Rightarrow\bigl(H_w'(x)\iff F'(x)\bigr).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology-dependent Hadamard semiderivatives of a function on a normed vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a normed vector space, let \(f\) be defined near \(x\in E\), and let \(v\in E\). When the respective limits exist, \[d_H^s f(x;v):=\lim_{\substack{t\searrow0\\w\to v\text{ strongly}}}\frac{f(x+tw)-f(x)}{t},\qquad d_H^w f(x;v):=\lim_{\substack{t\searrow0\\w\rightharpoonup v}}\frac{f(x+tw)-f(x)}{t}.\] Weak Hadamard semidifferentiability implies strong Hadamard semidifferentiability. In finite-dimensional \(E\), the two notions coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strong version permits norm-convergent perturbations of the direction, while the weak version requires the same limit for weakly convergent perturbations. The weak condition implies the strong condition, and they coincide in finite dimensions.
assumptions_latex: E\text{ is a normed vector space}
f\text{ is defined on a neighborhood of }x\in E
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_H^w f(x;v)\text{ exists}\Rightarrow d_H^s f(x;v)\text{ exists};\qquad \dim E<\infty\Rightarrow\bigl(d_H^w f(x;v)\text{ exists}\iff d_H^s f(x;v)\text{ exists}\bigr),\text{ and the values are equal.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz directional differentiability implies Hadamard differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional upgrade from fixed-direction differentiability to stability under perturbations of direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be directionally differentiable at $x$ and Lipschitz with constant $L$ on a neighborhood of $x$. Define $f'_x(g)=f'(x;g)$. Then $$|f'_x(g_1)-f'_x(g_2)|\le L\|g_1-g_2\|\qquad\forall g_1,g_2\in\mathbb R^n,$$ and $f$ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at $x$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is directionally differentiable at x and locally L-Lipschitz there, its directional derivative is L-Lipschitz as a function of direction, and f is Hadamard directionally differentiable at x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Lip}(f'_x)\le L\quad\text{and}\quad f\text{ is Hadamard directionally differentiable at }x

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and lower Hadamard directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper and lower Hadamard derivatives defined by perturbed-direction limsup and liminf.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\). The upper and lower Hadamard derivatives of \(f\) at \(x\) in direction \(g\) are \[f_H^{\uparrow}(x,g):=\limsup_{\substack{\alpha\downarrow0\\ g'\to g}}\frac{f(x+\alpha g')-f(x)}{\alpha},\qquad f_H^{\downarrow}(x,g):=\liminf_{\substack{\alpha\downarrow0\\ g'\to g}}\frac{f(x+\alpha g')-f(x)}{\alpha}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real-valued function on R^n, the upper and lower Hadamard derivatives are the limsup and liminf of the difference quotient as the positive step tends to zero and the perturbed direction approaches the specified direction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bouligand differentiability as a positively homogeneous first-order expansion.

source_refs.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\) if there exists a continuous positively homogeneous mapping \(F'_B(x;\cdot):X\to Y\) such that \[F(x+u)=F(x)+F'_B(x;u)+r(u),\qquad \lim_{\substack{u\to0\\u\ne0}}\frac{\|r(u)\|}{\|u\|}=0.\] Positive homogeneity means \(F'_B(x;\lambda h)=\lambda F'_B(x;h)\) for every \(h\in X\) and \(\lambda\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand differentiability supplies a continuous positively homogeneous first-order model whose approximation error is smaller than the increment norm.
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Directional Differentiability

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1.1 Generalized directional derivatives p. 159

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order chain rule for composable Bouligand-differentiable mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\) and \(G\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(F(x)\), then \(G\circ F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\), with \[(G\circ F)'_B(x;h)=G'_B\bigl(F(x);F'_B(x;h)\bigr)\qquad(h\in X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bouligand derivatives obey the ordinary composition rule, with the outer positively homogeneous model applied to the inner model.
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand Chain Rule

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bouligand differentiability is equivalent to a continuous positively homogeneous map giving all perturbed-direction quotient limits, and that map is unique.
review_flags: Finite dimensionality is essential to the stated equivalence from pointwise perturbed-direction limits to the uniform little-o expansion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equivalence between the uniform Bouligand expansion and a continuous all-direction Hadamard derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is Bouligand differentiable at \(x\) if and only if there exists a continuous positively homogeneous mapping \(A:X\to Y\) such that, for every \(h\in X\), every \(t_k\downarrow0\), and every \(h_k\to h\), \[\frac{F(x+t_kh_k)-F(x)}{t_k}\to A(h).\] In that case \(A\) is unique, \(A(h)=F'_B(x;h)=F'(x;h)\), and \[F(x+u)-F(x)-A(u)=o(\|u\|).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, Bouligand differentiability is equivalent to possessing one continuous positively homogeneous Hadamard derivative model in every direction; that model is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hadamard Characterization of the Bouligand Model

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Clarke generalized directional derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) in direction \(h\) is \[f^{\circ}(x;h)=\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(y+th)-f(y)}{t}.\] The base point may vary with the step, making this derivative robust under nearby perturbations. Local Lipschitz continuity ensures that \(f^{\circ}(x;h)\) is finite for every \(h\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke derivative takes the worst limiting directional growth over positive steps and nearby base points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Moving-Base Strictness for a Concave Corner
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Example separating robust nearby-base growth from fixed-base directional growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(u)=-|u|\), \[f'(0;h)=-|h|,\qquad f^{\circ}(0;h)=|h|.\] Thus the Clarke derivative strictly exceeds the fixed-base derivative whenever \(h\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a concave absolute-value corner, fixed-base growth is negative while robust nearby-base growth is positive.
knowledge_statements.title: Moving-Base Strictness for a Concave Corner

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical coincidence regimes for robust upper directional growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(x\), then \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle\). If \(f\) is convex and locally Lipschitz near \(x\), then \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=f'(x;h)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke derivative reduces to the gradient pairing for smooth functions and to the ordinary directional derivative for locally Lipschitz convex functions.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is either continuously Fréchet differentiable near \(x\), or convex and locally Lipschitz near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=\langle\nabla f(x),h\rangle\) in the smooth case and \(f^{\circ}(x;h)=f'(x;h)\) in the convex case.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core directional structure under local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is Lipschitz with constant \(L\) near \(x\), then \(h\mapsto f^{\circ}(x;h)\) is positively homogeneous and subadditive, and \[|f^{\circ}(x;h)|\le L\|h\|.\] Hence it is finite, continuous, and sublinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke derivative is a finite continuous sublinear function bounded by the local Lipschitz constant.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is Lipschitz with constant \(L\) near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{\circ}(x;\lambda h)=\lambda f^{\circ}(x;h)\), \(f^{\circ}(x;h+k)\le f^{\circ}(x;h)+f^{\circ}(x;k)\), and \(|f^{\circ}(x;h)|\le L\|h\|\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full-Measure Representation of the Clarke Upper Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation by upper Dini derivatives along an inner-full-measure subset of a Lipschitz neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined on an open set \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and be Lipschitz on a neighborhood \(S\) of \(x\in X\). If \(Q\subset S\) and the inner measure of \(S\setminus Q\) is zero, then, for every \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \[f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\uparrow}(x,g)=\limsup_{\substack{x'\to x\\x'\in Q}}f_D^{\uparrow}(x',g).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function Lipschitz near a point, the Clarke upper derivative equals the limsup of nearby upper Dini derivatives restricted to any subset whose complement has inner measure zero.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is Lipschitz on a neighborhood }S\text{ of }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_{\mathrm{Cl}}^{\uparrow}(x,g)=\limsup_{\substack{x'\to x\\x'\in Q}}f_D^{\uparrow}(x',g)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequences for the direction-dependent Clarke derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is locally Lipschitz at \(x\), then \(d\mapsto f^{\circ}(x;d)\) is convex, \(\operatorname{epi}f^{\circ}(x;\cdot)\) is a convex cone, and

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic Properties of the Clarke Generalized Directional Derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finiteness, sublinearity, upper semicontinuity, and Lipschitz bounds under local Lipschitz regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be Lipschitz near \(x\) with modulus \(\lambda\). Then \(h\mapsto f^0(x;h)\) is finite, positively homogeneous, and subadditive on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and
\[
|f^0(x;h)|\le \lambda\|h\|\qquad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Moreover, \(f^0(\cdot;\cdot)\) is upper semicontinuous at \((x,h)\) for every \(h\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(h\mapsto f^0(x;h)\) is Lipschitz on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with modulus \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If f is Lipschitz near x with modulus lambda, its Clarke generalized directional derivative at x is a finite sublinear function of the direction, is bounded and Lipschitz with modulus lambda, and is upper semicontinuous at every pair (x,h).
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is Lipschitz near }x\text{ with modulus }\lambda
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^0(x;\cdot)\text{ is finite, positively homogeneous, subadditive, and }\lambda\text{-Lipschitz};\quad |f^0(x;h)|\le\lambda\|h\|,\quad f^0(\cdot;\cdot)\text{ is upper semicontinuous at }(x,h).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke directional derivative and Clarke regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and support representation for locally Lipschitz real-valued functions on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $v:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R$ be locally Lipschitz and let $y^0,r\in\mathbb R^m$. The Clarke directional derivative is \[v^o(y^0;r)=\limsup_{\substack{y\to y^0\\ t\downarrow0}}\frac{v(y+tr)-v(y)}{t}.\] The function is Clarke regular at $y^0$ if $v'(y^0;r)$ exists and equals $v^o(y^0;r)$ for every $r\in\mathbb R^m$. Moreover, \[v^o(y^0;r)=\max_{\zeta\in\partial v(y^0)}\langle\zeta,r\rangle\qquad\forall r\in\mathbb R^m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke directional derivative is an upper limiting difference quotient in which both the base point and positive step vary. A locally Lipschitz function is Clarke regular at the reference point when every ordinary directional derivative exists and equals its Clarke derivative. The Clarke derivative is the support function of the Clarke generalized gradient.
assumptions_latex: v:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R\text{ is locally Lipschitz.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v^o(y^0;r)=\limsup_{\substack{y\to y^0\\ t\downarrow0}}\frac{v(y+tr)-v(y)}{t}=\max_{\zeta\in\partial v(y^0)}\langle\zeta,r\rangle;\quad v\text{ is Clarke regular at }y^0\iff \forall r,\ v'(y^0;r)\text{ exists and equals }v^o(y^0;r).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke Generalized Directional Derivative and Subdifferential Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robust upper directional growth and its characterization of the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), with \(\Omega\) open, be locally Lipschitz at \(x\in\Omega\). For each \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
g^\circ(x;d):=\limsup_{\substack{y\to x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{g(y+td)-g(y)}{t}.
\]
This value is finite, and
\[
\partial g(x)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb{R}^n:\xi^Td\le g^\circ(x;d)\ \text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized directional derivative is the upper limit of nearby forward difference quotients. Local Lipschitz continuity makes it finite, and the Clarke subdifferential comprises exactly the linear forms dominated by it in every direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad g^\circ(x;d)=\limsup_{y\to x,\,t\downarrow0}\frac{g(y+td)-g(y)}{t}\in\mathbb{R},\qquad \partial g(x)=\{\xi:\xi^Td\le g^\circ(x;d)\ \forall d\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic sufficient conditions for Clarke regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise regularity properties for locally Lipschitz functions and the resulting Clarke generalized-gradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be Lipschitz near \(x\). (a) If \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(x\), then \(f\) is regular at \(x\). (b) If \(f\) is convex, then \(f\) is regular at \(x\). (c) A finite linear combination with nonnegative coefficients of functions regular at \(x\) is regular at \(x\). (d) If \(f\) is regular at \(x\) and admits a Gâteaux derivative \(Df(x)\), then \(\partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict differentiability or convexity implies Clarke regularity at the point, and finite nonnegative linear combinations preserve regularity. If a regular function is Gâteaux differentiable there, its Clarke generalized gradient is the singleton containing that derivative.
assumptions_latex: \text{For (c), the functions are regular at }x\text{ and their coefficients are nonnegative}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Conclusions (a)--(c) give regularity at }x;\quad\text{conclusion (d) gives }\partial f(x)=\{Df(x)\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural relations between subderivatives and regular subderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower semicontinuity, positive homogeneity, ordering, sublinearity, and an epigraphical-limit representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\), both \(df(\bar x)\) and \(\widehat d f(\bar x)\) are lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous, and
\[
\widehat d f(\bar x)\ge df(\bar x).
\]
If \(f\) is lsc at \(\bar x\), then \(\widehat d f(\bar x)\) is sublinear. If \(f\) is locally lsc at \(\bar x\), then
\[
\widehat d f(\bar x)=\operatorname{e-limsup}_{x\to_f\bar x}df(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every finite-valued reference point, the ordinary and regular subderivatives are lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous, and the regular subderivative dominates the ordinary one. Lower semicontinuity at the point makes the regular subderivative sublinear; local lower semicontinuity also gives its epigraphical upper-limit representation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: df(\bar x),\widehat d f(\bar x)\text{ are lsc and positively homogeneous},\quad \widehat d f(\bar x)\ge df(\bar x);\quad f\text{ locally lsc at }\bar x\Rightarrow \widehat d f(\bar x)=\operatorname{e-limsup}_{x\to_f\bar x}df(x)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional derivative, sublinearity, regularity, and domain-interior identities for convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be convex and finite at \(\bar x\). For every \(w\in\mathbb R^n\), the limit
\[
h(w):=\lim_{\tau\searrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)}{\tau}
\]
exists and defines a sublinear extended-real function satisfying
\[
f(\bar x+\tau w)\ge f(\bar x)+\tau h(w)\qquad(\tau\ge0).
\]
Furthermore,
\[
\widehat d f(\bar x)(w)=df(\bar x)(w)=(\operatorname{cl}h)(w)\quad\text{for all }w.
\]
If
\[
W:=\{w:\exists\tau\ge0,\ \bar x+\tau w\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\},
\]
then \((\operatorname{cl}h)(w)=h(w)\) for \(w\in W\), and
\[
W=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\widehat d f(\bar x))=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}df(\bar x))=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex extended-real function finite at the reference point, every one-sided directional difference quotient has a limit. The resulting function is sublinear, gives a global raywise lower bound, and its lower-semicontinuous closure equals both the ordinary and regular subderivatives. On directions reaching the interior of the effective domain, no closure is needed, and this set is their common domain interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat d f(\bar x)=df(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}h,\quad h(w)=\lim_{\tau\searrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w)-f(\bar x)}{\tau}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(\bar x\) with \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\), let \(\Delta_\tau f(x)(w):=[f(x+\tau w)-f(x)]/\tau\). The regular subderivative function is defined by
\[
\widehat d f(\bar x):=\operatorname{e-limsup}_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\x\to_f\bar x}}\Delta_\tau f(x),

where \(x\to_f\bar x\) denotes functional convergence: \(x\to\bar x\) and \(f(x)\to f(\bar x)\).

The resulting mapping \(h\mapsto F'(x;h)\) is positively homogeneous. In finite dimensions, this is equivalent to convergence for arbitrary sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(h_k\to h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is semidifferentiable at the fixed base point when every direction has a common directional limit stable under perturbations of that direction; the resulting model is positively homogeneous.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is semidifferentiable at \(x\) with derivative \(D\) if and only if \(D:X\to Y\) is continuous and positively homogeneous and \[F(x+u)=F(x)+D(u)+o(\bigl(\|u\|\bigr)\qquad(u\to0).\] In that case \(D(h)=F'(x;h)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semidifferentiability is equivalent to a uniform first-order expansion with a continuous positively homogeneous model.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional normed spaces and \(F:X\to Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x+u)-F(x)-F'(x;u)=o(\|u\|)\), and \(F'(x;\cdot)\) is continuous and positively homogeneous.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition rule for fixed-base Hadamard semiderivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F:X\to Y\) is semidifferentiable at \(x\) and \(G:Y\to Z\) is semidifferentiable at \(F(x)\), then \(G\circ F\) is semidifferentiable at \(x\) and \[(G\circ F)'(x;h)=G'(F(x);F'(x;h)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semiderivatives compose by applying the outer semiderivative to the inner semiderivative.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is semidifferentiable at \(x\), and \(G\) is semidifferentiable at \(F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((G\circ F)'(x;h)=G'(F(x);F'(x;h))\) for every \(h\in X\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perturbation-stable directional derivative of an extended-real-valued function at a finite-valued point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} with f(\bar x) finite. If, for w\in\mathbb{R}^n, the possibly infinite limit \[\mathrm{d}f(\bar x)(w):=\lim_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w')-f(\bar x)}{\tau}\] exists, it is the semiderivative of f at \bar x for w, and f is semidifferentiable at \bar x for w. The function f is semidifferentiable at \bar x if this holds for every w\in\mathbb{R}^n.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point where f is finite, the semiderivative for w is the possibly infinite difference-quotient limit as the positive step tends to zero while the perturbed direction tends to w. Semidifferentiability at the point requires this limit for every direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{d}f(\bar x)(w)=\lim_{\substack{\tau\searrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+\tau w')-f(\bar x)}{\tau};\qquad f\text{ is semidifferentiable at }\bar x\iff\text{the limit exists for every }w.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contingent epiderivative of an interval-valued mapping at its lower endpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and representation for an interval-valued multifunction whose lower endpoint function is convex and continuous at the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(X,\|\cdot\|_X)$ be a real normed space, let $f,g:X\to\mathbb{R}$, and define $F:X\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}$ by $$F(x):=\{y\in\mathbb{R}\mid f(x)\leq y\leq g(x)\}\quad\text{for every }x\in X.$$ Let $\bar{x}\in X$. If $f$ is continuous at $\bar{x}$ and convex, then the contingent epiderivative of $F$ at $(\bar{x},f(\bar{x}))$ exists and equals the directional derivative of $f$ at $\bar{x}$: $$DF(\bar{x},f(\bar{x}))(h)=f'(\bar{x})(h)\quad\text{for every }h\in X.$$

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DF(\bar{x},f(\bar{x}))\text{ exists and }\forall h\in X,\quad DF(\bar{x},f(\bar{x}))(h)=f'(\bar{x})(h).

knowledge_statements.title: Lower Epiderivative Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower perturbed-direction first-order regime for an extended-real function on a finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and suppose \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\). For \(t>0\), define \[q_t(h):=\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] The lower Hadamard epiderivative is \[d^-f(\bar x;h):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}q_t(h')=\sup_{\varepsilon>0}\inf\{q_t(h'):0<t<\varepsilon,\ \|h'-h\|<\varepsilon\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower Hadamard epiderivative is the liminf of first-order difference quotients under simultaneous vanishing steps and directional perturbations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^-f(\bar x;h)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0,\,h'\to h}q_t(h')\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\underline d_D f(\bar x;h):=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)}{t}.\] Then \[d^-f(\bar x;h)\le \underline d_D f(\bar x;h).\] Equality holds whenever the lower first-order behavior is stable under perturbations of the direction; in particular, equality holds when the corresponding Hadamard directional limit exists at \(h\).

knowledge_statements.title: Epiderivative Coincidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise coincidence of lower and upper Hadamard epiderivatives in a fixed direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) satisfy \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\), and fix \(h\in X\). With \[q_t(h'):=\frac{f(\bar x+th')-f(\bar x)}{t},\] one has \[d^-f(\bar x;h)\le d^+f(\bar x;h).\] Moreover, for \(a\in[-\infty,+\infty]\), \[d^-f(\bar x;h)=d^+f(\bar x;h)=a\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lim_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\h'\to h}}q_t(h')=a\] in the extended real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower and upper Hadamard epiderivatives coincide at an extended-real value exactly when the perturbed first-order quotient converges to that value.
assumptions_latex: \(h\in X\), and both epiderivatives use the same perturbed-direction convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^-f(\bar x;h)=d^+f(\bar x;h)\) if and only if the corresponding perturbed-direction quotient has an extended-real limit.

children.top_down_role: Asymmetric limiting behavior preventing a single epiderivative model.

assumptions_latex: \(d^-f(\bar x;h)\) and \(d^+f(\bar x;h)\) use the same positive-step, perturbed-direction convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict separation of the lower and upper values is exactly failure of the perturbed-direction quotient to have an extended-real limit; when both endpoints are finite their difference is a positive scalar gap.
review_flags: This corrects the deferred seed by distinguishing scalar quotient nonconvergence from failure or nonuniqueness of an epigraphical set limit.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of one perturbed-direction first-order limit through strict lower-upper separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[q_t(h'):=\frac{f(\bar x+th')-f(\bar x)}{t},\] one always has \(d^-f(\bar x;h)\le d^+f(\bar x;h)\). If both endpoints are finite, define \[G(\bar x;h):=d^+f(\bar x;h)-d^-f(\bar x;h).\] Then \(G(\bar x;h)>0\) if and only if \(q_t(h')\) has no limit as \(t\downarrow0\) and \(h'\to h\). More generally, unequal extended-real endpoints imply the same nonconvergence, but no numerical gap is defined when extended-real subtraction is indeterminate. This conclusion concerns the scalar joint limit and does not by itself assert failure or nonuniqueness of a Painleve-Kuratowski epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different lower and upper perturbed-direction values prevent a single first-order quotient limit; a numerical gap is used only when both endpoints are finite.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G(\bar x;h):=d^+f(\bar x;h)-d^-f(\bar x;h)>0\) signals a nonunique first-order epigraphical limit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(d^-f(\bar x;h)\) and \(d^+f(\bar x;h)\) are finite. Their epigraphical limit gap is \[G(\bar x;h):=d^+f(\bar x;h)-d^-f(\bar x;h)\ge0.\] If \(G(\bar x;h)>0\), there exist sequences \(t_k\downarrow0\), \(h_k\to h\) and \(s_k\downarrow0\), \(v_k\to h\) along which the corresponding difference quotients approach distinct cluster values. children.title: Epi-Differentiability
children.top_down_role: Stable epigraphical first-order approximation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is properly epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) when \(q_t\) epi-converges to a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(d_e f(\bar x)\).
review_flags: Uses the explicit proper epi-differentiability convention to avoid conflating proper and possibly improper epi-limits.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper first-order epi-differentiability through Painleve-Kuratowski convergence of difference-quotient epigraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is properly epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) if there exists a proper lower-semicontinuous function \(d_e f(\bar x):X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \[q_t\xrightarrow{e}d_e f(\bar x)\quad\text{as }t\downarrow0.\] Equivalently, \(\operatorname{epi}q_t\) converges to \(\operatorname{epi}d_e f(\bar x)\) in the Painleve-Kuratowski sense. The limit is unique and is the proper first epi-derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proper epi-differentiability means that the first-order difference quotients epi-converge to one proper lower-semicontinuous function.
knowledge_statements.title: Proper First Epi-Differentiability

assumptions_latex: The assumptions and notation of proper first epi-differentiability hold.
Convergence is interpreted sequentially in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_t\xrightarrow{e}g\) exactly when every vanishing-scale convergent-direction sequence satisfies the liminf inequality and every direction has recovery directions along every vanishing scale sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization and failure boundary for the first-order quotient family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower-semicontinuous \(g\), the convergence \(q_t\xrightarrow{e}g\) as \(t\downarrow0\) is equivalent to both conditions: (i) for every \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(h_k\to h\), \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}q_{t_k}(h_k)\ge g(h);\] and (ii) for every \(h\) and every \(t_k\downarrow0\), there exist \(h_k\to h\) such that \[\limsup_{k\to\infty}q_{t_k}(h_k)\le g(h).\] Thus proper epi-differentiability fails exactly when no single proper lower-semicontinuous \(g\) satisfies both requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epi-differentiability is characterized by a universal lower-limit inequality and recovery directions along every vanishing sequence of scales.
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Epi-Differentiability Test

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional, \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, and \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.title: Directionally Regular Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke directional regularity for finite-valued locally Lipschitz functions on finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\). Suppose that for every \(h\in X\) the directional derivative \[f'(\bar x;h):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)}{t}\] exists. Define the Clarke generalized directional derivative by \[f^{\circ}(\bar x;h):=\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{f(x+th)-f(x)}{t}.\] The function \(f\) is directionally regular at \(\bar x\) if \[f'(\bar x;h)=f^{\circ}(\bar x;h)\quad\text{for every }h\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function is directionally regular at a point when each ordinary directional derivative exists and equals the corresponding Clarke generalized directional derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is directionally regular at \(\bar x\) when \(f'(\bar x;h)=f^{\circ}(\bar x;h)\) for every \(h\in X\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(0;h)=-|h|\ne |h|=f^\circ(0;h)\) for \(h\ne0\), so \(f\) is not directionally regular at \(0\).

Clarke generalized directional derivative at zero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp counterexample showing that local Lipschitz continuity and existence of all directional derivatives do not imply directional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=-|x|\), the ordinary directional derivative exists in every direction and equals \[f'(0;h)=-|h|.\] The Clarke generalized directional derivative is \[f^\circ(0;h)=|h|.\] Thus the two derivatives disagree for every \(h\ne0\), and \(f\) is not directionally regular at zero. Equivalently, the ordinary directional derivative is not sublinear and therefore cannot be a support function. This also shows that negation need not preserve directional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The locally Lipschitz function minus absolute value has all ordinary directional derivatives, but they equal minus absolute value rather than the Clarke derivative absolute value.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional Differentiability Does Not Imply Regularity
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Differentiability Does Not Imply Regularity

assumptions_latex: The functions under consideration are finite-valued and locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C^1\text{ functions and locally Lipschitz convex functions are directionally regular at }\bar x.

notation.meaning: Convex subdifferential, equal here to the Clarke subdifferential

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical smooth and convex regimes in which ordinary and Clarke directional constructions coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), then \[f'(\bar x;h)=f^\circ(\bar x;h)=\langle\nabla f(\bar x),h\rangle.\] If \(f\) is convex and locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\), then \[f'(\bar x;h)=f^\circ(\bar x;h)=\max_{v\in\partial f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle.\] Hence both classes are directionally regular at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuously differentiable functions and locally Lipschitz convex functions are directionally regular, with gradient and subgradient support formulas respectively.
knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Smooth and Convex Regimes

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) and directionally regular at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(\bar x;h)=\sigma_{\partial^C f(\bar x)}(h)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle\) for every \(h\), and \(h\mapsto f'(\bar x;h)\) is finite, continuous, and sublinear.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent dual representation and immediate structural consequences of Clarke directional regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite-valued locally Lipschitz function on a finite-dimensional space, \(f^\circ(\bar x;h)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle\). Consequently, \(f\) is directionally regular at \(\bar x\) if and only if its ordinary directional derivative exists in every direction and satisfies \[f'(\bar x;h)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,h\rangle\quad\text{for all }h.\] In that case \(h\mapsto f'(\bar x;h)\) is a finite continuous sublinear function. In particular, an existing directional derivative that is not sublinear cannot be directionally regular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a directionally regular point, the ordinary directional derivative is exactly the support function of the Clarke subdifferential and is therefore continuous and sublinear.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke-Subdifferential Support Representation

assumptions_latex: \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to\mathbb R\) are locally Lipschitz and directionally regular at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_i\lambda_i f_i\) and \(\max_i f_i\) are directionally regular at \(\bar x\), with the stated derivative formulas.

notation.meaning: Indices attaining the finite maximum at the base point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary closure calculus for Clarke-directionally regular locally Lipschitz functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) be locally Lipschitz and directionally regular at \(\bar x\). For coefficients \(\lambda_i\ge0\), the function \(g=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i\) is directionally regular and \[g'(\bar x;h)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f_i'(\bar x;h).\] The finite maximum \(F=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\) is also directionally regular and \[F'(\bar x;h)=\max_{i\in I(\bar x)}f_i'(\bar x;h),\qquad I(\bar x)=\{i:f_i(\bar x)=F(\bar x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative finite sums and finite maxima preserve directional regularity, with sum and active-index maximum derivative formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure Under Nonnegative Sums and Finite Maxima
knowledge_statements.title: Closure Under Nonnegative Sums and Finite Maxima

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional regularity characterized by equality of the ordinary and Clarke generalized directional derivatives, with immediate closure and representation properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz on the open set \(\Omega\). It is Clarke regular at \(x\in\Omega\) if it is directionally differentiable at \(x\) and
\[
g^\circ(x;d)=g'(x;d)\qquad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
Convex functions and functions continuously differentiable at \(x\) are Clarke regular there, and nonnegative combinations of functions regular at the same point are regular. Under Clarke regularity at \(x\),
\[
g'(x;d)=\max_{\xi\in\partial g(x)}\xi^Td\qquad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function is Clarke regular at a point when it is directionally differentiable there and its ordinary and Clarke directional derivatives agree in every direction. Convex and continuously differentiable functions are regular, nonnegative combinations preserve regularity, and regularity gives a support formula through the Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is Clarke regular at }x\iff g\text{ is directionally differentiable at }x\text{ and }g^\circ(x;d)=g'(x;d)\ \forall d;\quad g'(x;d)=\max_{\xi\in\partial g(x)}\xi^Td\text{ under regularity}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is subdifferentially regular at \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) if it is locally Lipschitz at \(x\) and, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the directional derivative \(f'(x;d)\) exists and satisfies \(f'(x;d)=f^\circ(x;d)\). Directional differentiability alone is insufficient, as shown by minus absolute value at zero.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke regularity of a locally Lipschitz function and the stated almost-everywhere consequence when regularity holds globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^N\to\mathbb{R}\) be locally Lipschitz. The function \(f\) is subdifferentially regular at \(x\) if, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^N\), the ordinary directional derivative \(f'(x;d)\) exists and satisfies \(f'(x;d)=f^{\circ}(x;d)\). If this equality holds at every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^N\) for every direction \(d\), then the Clarke subdifferential \(\partial^C f(x)\) is a singleton for almost every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz function is subdifferentially regular at x when all ordinary directional derivatives exist there and equal the Clarke generalized directional derivatives. If this regularity holds everywhere, its Clarke subdifferential is singleton-valued almost everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is subdifferentially regular at }x\iff\forall d\in\mathbb{R}^N,\ f'(x;d)\text{ exists and }f'(x;d)=f^{\circ}(x;d);\quad [\forall x,d,\ f'(x;d)=f^{\circ}(x;d)]\Rightarrow\partial^C f(x)\text{ is a singleton for a.e. }x

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Smooth Directional Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite continuous selections of smooth functions and their branchwise first-order models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open. A continuous function \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is piecewise smooth if there are finitely many functions \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m\in C^1(U)\) such that \[f(x)\in\{\phi_1(x),\ldots,\phi_m(x)\}\quad\text{for every }x\in U.\] Define \[I(x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:f(x)=\phi_i(x)\}.\] If \(i\in I(\bar x)\), \(t_k\downarrow0\), \(h_k\to h\), and \(f(\bar x+t_kh_k)=\phi_i(\bar x+t_kh_k)\), then \[\frac{f(\bar x+t_kh_k)-f(\bar x)}{t_k}\to\nabla\phi_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}h.\] Thus branchwise first-order limits are drawn from finitely many linear models.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-smooth function selects among finitely many smooth pieces; along a sequence that remains on one active piece, its first-order quotient converges to that piece's linearization.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
\(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m\in C^1(U)\) are finitely many selections satisfying \(f(x)\in\{\phi_1(x),\ldots,\phi_m(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If a sequence approaching \(\bar x\) in direction \(h\) remains on an active branch \(i\), its first-order quotient converges to \(\nabla\phi_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}h\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order regularity forced by a finite continuous piecewise-C1 scalar selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be a continuous selection of finitely many \(C^1\) functions \(\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_m\). Then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and Bouligand differentiable at every \(\bar x\in U\). Its derivative \(f'_B(\bar x;\cdot)\) is continuous, positively homogeneous, and piecewise linear, and \[f'_B(\bar x;h)\in\{\nabla\phi_i(\bar x)^{\mathsf T}h:i\in I(\bar x)\}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^n).\] Moreover, \[f(\bar x+u)=f(\bar x)+f'_B(\bar x;u)+o(\|u\|).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite continuous piecewise-C1 scalar selection is locally Lipschitz and Bouligand differentiable, with a continuous piecewise-linear derivative selected from active branch linearizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Limit Nonexistence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous one-dimensional counterexample to existence of a one-sided directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \[f(0)=0,\qquad f(x)=x\sin(\log(1/|x|))\quad(x\ne0).\] The function is continuous at \(0\), while its directional quotient in direction \(1\) satisfies \[\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}=-1<1=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}.\] Therefore \(f'(0;1)\) does not exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This continuous oscillatory function has directional quotients with lower limit −1 and upper limit 1, so its directional derivative at zero in direction one does not exist.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x\sin(\log(1/|x|))\) for \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(0;1)\) does not exist.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Limit Oscillation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent bounded oscillation separating lower and upper directional limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \[f(0)=0,\qquad f(x)=x\sin(1/x)\quad(x\ne0).\] Its fixed-direction quotient satisfies \[\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}=-1<1=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}.\] Under the perturbed-direction Hadamard convention, the same endpoint values hold at direction \(1\): \[d^-f(0;1)=-1<1=d^+f(0;1).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For this function the quotient oscillates persistently between −1 and 1; both the fixed-direction and perturbed-direction lower and upper limits remain separated.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x\sin(1/x)\) for \(x\ne0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Base-Point Instability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing directional derivatives at one point with unbounded classical derivatives at nearby base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \[f(0)=0,\qquad f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)\quad(x\ne0).\] Then \[f'(0;h)=0\quad\text{for every }h\in\mathbb R,\] whereas for \(x\ne0\), \[f'(x)=2x\sin(1/x^2)-\frac{2}{x}\cos(1/x^2),\] and \(f'\) is unbounded on every neighborhood of \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every directional derivative at zero vanishes, but the classical derivatives at nearby nonzero points are unbounded.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)=x^2\sin(1/x^2)\) for \(x\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'(0;h)=0\) for every \(h\in\mathbb R\), but \(f'\) is unbounded on every neighborhood of \(0\).

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Model Breakdown
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hölder growth below order one prevents a finite directional model at linear scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(f(x)=|x|^{1/2}\). For every \(h\ne0\), \[\frac{f(th)-f(0)}{t}=|h|^{1/2}t^{-1/2}\to+\infty\quad\text{as }t\downarrow0.\] Thus no finite-valued first-order directional model at scale \(t\) represents the nonzero directions at the origin.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the square-root function every nonzero directional quotient diverges to positive infinity at linear scale, so no finite first-order directional model exists there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{t\downarrow0}[f(th)-f(0)]/t=+\infty\) for every \(h\ne0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous two-dimensional example separating existence of all fixed-ray directional derivatives from a uniform first-order approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f(0,0)=0,\qquad f(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,\frac{x^3y}{x^6+y^2}\quad ((x,y)\ne(0,0)).\] The fraction has absolute value at most \(1/2\), so \(f\) is continuous at the origin. For every fixed \(h\in\mathbb R^2\), \(f'(0;h)=0\). Nevertheless, along \(z_s=(s,s^3)\), \[\frac{f(z_s)-f(0)-f'(0;z_s)}{\|z_s\|}=\frac12\] for every \(s\ne0\). Thus the pointwise directional derivative exists in every direction but does not give a uniform first-order approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All fixed-ray directional derivatives at the origin are zero, yet along a curved approach the normalized error remains one half, so the zero directional model is not a uniform first-order model.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(\bar x)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n: f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\ \text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\}\).

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 Basic Definitions and Representations p. 40

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the convex subdifferential is
\[
\partial f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\ \text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
Thus \(v\) is a convex subgradient exactly when the affine function with slope \(v\) passing through \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\) globally minorizes \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subgradient is the slope of an affine function supporting the graph from below at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subdifferential

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\partial f(\bar x)\iff\bar x\in\operatorname{argmin}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global-optimality certificate for proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper convex function \(f\) and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[0\in\partial f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(\bar x)=\inf_x f(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function, zero is a subgradient exactly at its global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Fermat Certificate

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\partial f(x)\iff f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle v,x\rangle\iff x\in\partial f^*(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proper closed convex functions in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), \[v\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(x)+f^*(v)=\langle v,x\rangle\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\partial f^*(v).\] Hence \((\partial f)^{-1}=\partial f^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subgradient membership is equality in Fenchel-Young, and conjugacy reverses the subdifferential relation.
knowledge_statements.title: Fenchel-Young Subgradient Equivalences

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\Rightarrow\partial f(x)\ne\varnothing\); if \(f\) is finite near \(x\), differentiability at \(x\) is equivalent to \(\partial f(x)\) being a singleton.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise finite-dimensional structure of a proper convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\), \(\partial f(x)\) is closed and convex, and it is nonempty when \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). If \(f\) is finite on a neighborhood of \(x\), then \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) if and only if \(\partial f(x)\) is a singleton, in which case \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\). At boundary points of the domain the subdifferential can be empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subgradients exist throughout the relative interior, and a singleton subdifferential characterizes differentiability at locally finite points.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonemptiness and Differentiability Tests

assumptions_latex: All spaces are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is maximally cyclically monotone if and only if \(T=\partial f\) for a proper closed convex function \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization of convex subdifferential mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every proper closed convex function \(f\), the mapping \(\partial f\) is maximally cyclically monotone. Conversely, \(T:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^n\) is maximally cyclically monotone if and only if \(T=\partial f\) for some proper closed convex function \(f\); the potential is unique up to an additive constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex subdifferentials are precisely the maximally cyclically monotone mappings.
knowledge_statements.title: Maximal Cyclic Monotonicity

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space, let \(f:X\to\mathbb R_\infty\) be convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). If \(f\) is Gâteaux differentiable at \(x\), then \[\partial f(x)=\{f'_G(x)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a domain point where a convex function is Gâteaux differentiable, its subdifferential consists exactly of its Gâteaux derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{f'_G(x)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of an Affine Infinity Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit convex-subdifferential formula for the infinity norm of an affine mapping, including the zero-residual case. This is extraction-grounded evidence without verified item-span alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be defined by f(x)=\|Ax+b\|_\infty, where A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, b\in\mathbb{R}^m, and a_i^T is the i-th row of A. Define I_x=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}:|a_i^Tx+b_i|=\|Ax+b\|_\infty\}. Then
\[
\partial f(x)=\begin{cases}
A^T B_{\|\cdot\|_1}[0,1],&Ax+b=0,\\
\left\{\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I_x}\lambda_i\operatorname{sgn}(a_i^Tx+b_i)a_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \displaystyle\sum_{i\in I_x}\lambda_i=1\right\},&Ax+b\neq0.
\end{cases}
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the infinity norm of an affine mapping, the subdifferential at a nonzero residual is the convex hull of the signed active rows of the matrix. At a zero residual, it is the image under the matrix transpose of the closed unit ball for the l1 norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\begin{cases}A^T B_{\|\cdot\|_1}[0,1],&Ax+b=0,\\ \left\{\sum_{i\in I_x}\lambda_i\operatorname{sgn}(a_i^Tx+b_i)a_i:\lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i\in I_x}\lambda_i=1\right\},&Ax+b\neq0.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Top-Eigenvector Subgradient of an Affine Maximum-Eigenvalue Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of one convex subgradient of the maximum eigenvalue of an affine symmetric-matrix mapping; it is not a complete representation of the subdifferential when the top eigenvalue has multiplicity. This is extraction-grounded evidence without verified item-span alignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let A_0,A_1,\ldots,A_m\in\mathbb{S}^n and define \mathcal{A}:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{S}^n by \mathcal{A}(x)=A_0+\sum_{i=1}^m x_iA_i. Let f(x)=\lambda_{\max}(\mathcal{A}(x)). For any x\in\mathbb{R}^m, let \tilde y be a normalized eigenvector of \mathcal{A}(x) corresponding to \lambda_{\max}(\mathcal{A}(x)). Then
\[
(\tilde y^TA_1\tilde y,\tilde y^TA_2\tilde y,\ldots,\tilde y^TA_m\tilde y)^T\in\partial f(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the maximum eigenvalue of an affine symmetric-matrix mapping, any unit eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue yields a subgradient whose coordinates are its quadratic forms with the coefficient matrices. This constructs a subgradient rather than characterizing the entire subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\tilde y^TA_1\tilde y,\tilde y^TA_2\tilde y,\ldots,\tilde y^TA_m\tilde y)^T\in\partial f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper convex function \(\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), \[y\in\partial\varphi(x)\iff \varphi(z)\geq\varphi(x)+\langle y,z-xangle\quad orall z\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] The mapping may be identified with its graph. If \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\varphi)\), then \(\partial\varphi(x)
eq\varnothing\), and \(\varphi\) is differentiable at \(x\) iff \(\partial\varphi(x)=\{
abla\varphi(x)\}\). If \(\varphi\) is also lower semicontinuous, then \[x_k	o x,\quad y_k	o y,\quad y_k\in\partial\varphi(x_k)\ \Longrightarrow\ y\in\partial\varphi(x).\] For \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\varphi)\), \[\partial\varphi(x)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}\left\{\lim_k
abla\varphi(x_k):x_k	o x,\ \varphi	ext{ is differentiable at }x_kight\}.\] If additionally \(\varphi(x)>\inf\varphi\) and \(C_x=\{z:\varphi(z)\leq\varphi(x)\}\), then \(N_{C_x}(x)=\operatorname{cone}(\partial\varphi(x))\); this equality is not guaranteed at a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex subgradient defines a global supporting affine function. Interior-domain subdifferentials are nonempty, singleton values characterize differentiability, and lower semicontinuity gives a closed graph. The subdifferential is also the closed convex hull of reachable gradients. At a nonminimal level it generates the normal cone to the sublevel set, while this normal-cone equality may fail at a minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence, weak-star compactness, and Lipschitz bound for convex subgradients

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subderivatives and the Subdifferential on the Real Line
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional definition of the convex subdifferential using the left and right derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\operatorname{Conv}\mathbb R\) and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). A scalar \(s\in\mathbb R\) is a subderivative of \(f\) at \(x\) when \[D_-f(x)\le s\le D_+f(x).\] The subdifferential is the set of all such subderivatives: \[\partial f(x)=\{s\in\mathbb R:D_-f(x)\le s\le D_+f(x)\}.\] If both one-sided derivatives are finite, then \[\partial f(x)=[D_-f(x),D_+f(x)].\]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition by global affine support, together with its epigraph interpretation and basic set properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space, \(f:X\to\mathbb R_\infty\), and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). A functional \(\zeta\in X^*\) is a convex-analytic subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\) if \[f(y)-f(x)\geq\langle\zeta,y-x\rangle\qquad\forall y\in X.\] Equivalently, \(y\mapsto f(x)+\langle\zeta,y-x\rangle\) supports \(f\) at \(x\), and the corresponding hyperplane supports \(\operatorname{epi}f\) at \((x,f(x))\). The subdifferential is \[\partial f(x):=\{\zeta\in X^*:f(y)-f(x)\geq\langle\zeta,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\in X\}.\] It is convex and weak-star closed, and \(x\mapsto\partial f(x)\) is a set-valued map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-analytic subgradient is a continuous linear functional whose affine function globally supports the given function at the point. All such functionals form a convex, weak-star closed subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f(x)=\{\zeta\in X^*:f(y)-f(x)\geq\langle\zeta,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\in X\}\text{ is convex and weak-star closed}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the proximal subdifferential is
\[
\partial_P f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \exists r>0,\ \exists\delta>0:\ f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle-\frac r2\|x-\bar x\|^2\ \text{whenever }\|x-\bar x\|<\delta\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\partial_P f(\bar x)\) when \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle+(r/2)\|x-\bar x\|^2\) for some \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal subgradient supplies a local affine lower support after allowing a negative quadratic error.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular, Limiting, and Singular Subdifferential Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential construction of limiting and singular subgradients from regular or vanishing-error regular subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\), define
\[\widehat\partial\varphi(x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\liminf_{\substack{u\to x,\ u\ne x}}\frac{\varphi(u)-\varphi(x)-\langle v,u-x\rangle}{\|u-x\|}\ge0\right\}.\]
Writing \(x_k\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x\) when \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(\varphi(x_k)\to\varphi(\bar x)\),
\[\partial\varphi(\bar x)=\left\{v:\exists x_k\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x,\ \exists v_k\in\widehat\partial\varphi(x_k),\ v_k\to v\right\},\]
\[\partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)=\left\{v:\exists x_k\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x,\ \exists\lambda_k\downarrow0,\ \exists v_k\to v,\ v_k\in\lambda_k\widehat\partial\varphi(x_k)\right\}.\]
Both representations remain valid when the regular subdifferentials are replaced by their \(\varepsilon_k\)-enlargements, defined by replacing the lower bound \(0\) by \(-\varepsilon_k\), provided \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular subdifferential is defined by a first-order lower-support inequality. Limiting subgradients are limits of regular subgradients along points converging both in argument and function value. Singular subgradients are limits of vanishing positive scalings of such regular subgradients. Vanishing-error regular subgradients give the same representations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial\varphi(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x}\widehat\partial\varphi(x),\qquad \partial^\infty\varphi(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\xrightarrow{\varphi}\bar x\\ \lambda\downarrow0}}\lambda\widehat\partial\varphi(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximation of subgradients under uniform semiconvex convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability of subgradients for uniformly convergent semiconvex functions on a Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) be open in a Riemannian manifold and let \((\psi_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) be semiconvex functions converging uniformly to \(\psi\) on \(U\). For every \(\bar x\in U\) and every \(p\in\nabla^-\psi(\bar x)\), there exist \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(p_k\in\nabla^-\psi_k(x_k)\) such that \(p_k\to p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under uniform convergence of semiconvex functions, every subgradient of the limit at a given point can be approximated by subgradients of the approximating functions at nearby points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet Differentiability via Lower and Upper Fréchet Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint nonemptiness characterizes Fréchet differentiability; a one-sided singleton condition does not suffice.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi:X	o\overline{\mathbb R}\) satisfy \(|\varphi( ar x)|<\infty\). Then \(\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)
eq\varnothing\) and \(\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi( ar x)
eq\varnothing\) if and only if \(\varphi\) is Fréchet differentiable at \( ar x\). In that case, \(\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)=\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi( ar x)=\{
abla\varphi( ar x)\}\). Hence, if either subdifferential is not a singleton, the other is empty. A singleton in only one construction is insufficient: for \(\varphi(x)=\max\{0,x\sin(1/x)\}\) when \(x
eq0\) and \(\varphi(0)=0\), \(\widehat\partial\varphi(0)=\{0\}\) while \(\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi(0)=\varnothing\), and \(\varphi\) is not Fréchet differentiable at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-valued function is Fréchet differentiable at a point exactly when both its lower and upper Fréchet subdifferentials are nonempty; both then equal the singleton containing the gradient. A singleton in only one of the two subdifferentials does not imply differentiability, as the stated oscillatory example demonstrates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)
eq\varnothing\ \land\ \widehat\partial^{+}\varphi( ar x)
eq\varnothing\iff\varphi	ext{ is Fréchet differentiable at } ar x\), and then \(\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)=\widehat\partial^{+}\varphi( ar x)=\{
abla\varphi( ar x)\}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fréchet Subdifferential and Its Proper Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition for proper lower-semicontinuous extended-real-valued functionals on a Hilbert space. The extracted equivalent small-o formula is omitted because its limit expression is truncated.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X$ be a Hilbert space and let $\phi:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and lower semicontinuous. The Fréchet subdifferential is defined by
\[
\xi\in\partial\phi(v)\iff v\in D(\phi)\ \text{and}\ \liminf_{w\to v}\frac{\phi(w)-\phi(v)-\langle\xi,w-v\rangle}{\lVert w-v\rVert}\ge 0.
\]
Its proper domain is
\[
D(\partial\phi):=\{v\in X:\partial\phi(v)\neq\varnothing\}\subseteq D(\phi).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a Fréchet subgradient at a finite-valued point when the normalized first-order linearization error has nonnegative lower limit. The proper domain of the subdifferential consists of points possessing at least one such subgradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \xi\in\partial\phi(v)\iff v\in D(\phi)\ \text{and}\ \liminf_{w\to v}\frac{\phi(w)-\phi(v)-\langle\xi,w-v\rangle}{\lVert w-v\rVert}\ge0,\qquad D(\partial\phi)=\{v\in X:\partial\phi(v)\neq\varnothing\}\subseteq D(\phi).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable-minorant, smooth-support, and global bump-function representations of Fréchet subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\varphi:X	o\overline{\mathbb R}\) be proper and finite at \( ar x\). If \(s\) is defined near \( ar x\), is Fréchet differentiable at \( ar x\), satisfies \(
abla s( ar x)=x^*\), and \(\varphi-s\) has a local minimum at \( ar x\), then \(x^*\in\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)\). Conversely, every \(x^*\in\widehat\partial\varphi( ar x)\) is the derivative at \( ar x\) of a function \(s:X	o\mathbb R\) satisfying \(s( ar x)=\varphi( ar x)\) and \(s\leq\varphi\). If \(X\) admits an \(\mathcal S\)-smooth bump function, \(\mathcal S\in\{\mathcal F,\mathcal{LF},\mathcal{LC}^1\}\), then there is an \(\mathcal S\)-smooth local function \(s\) with \(
abla s( ar x)=x^*\) and \(\varphi(x)-s(x)-\|x- ar x\|^2\geq\varphi( ar x)-s( ar x)\) locally. If \(X\) admits a Fréchet-smooth renorm, this \(s\) can be concave, and if additionally \(\varphi\) is bounded below it can be defined with the inequality on all of \(X\). If \(\varphi\) is bounded below and \(X\) admits the stated smooth bump function, there is a bump function \(b\) with \(
abla b( ar x)=x^*\) such that \(\varphi-b\) has a global minimum at \( ar x\); moreover, suitable global \(\mathcal S\)-smooth \(s\) and \(	heta\) satisfy \(
abla s( ar x)=x^*\), \(	heta(x)=0\iff x=0\), \(	heta(x)\leq\|x\|^2\) for \(\|x\|\leq1\), and \(\varphi(x)-s(x)-	heta(x- ar x)\geq\varphi( ar x)-s( ar x)\) for all \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable local support produces a Fréchet subgradient, and every Fréchet subgradient is represented by a differentiable global minorant. Smooth bump-function and boundedness assumptions yield the stronger local and global support representations stated above.
assumptions_latex: \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) is proper and finite at \(\bar x\).
The smooth-support conclusions assume that \(X\) admits an \(\mathcal S\)-smooth bump function for \(\mathcal S\in\{\mathcal F,\mathcal{LF},\mathcal{LC}^1\}\).
Concavity assumes a Fréchet-smooth renorm; the global conclusions additionally assume that \(\varphi\) is bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fréchet subgradients admit the stated differentiable-minorant and, under the additional hypotheses, smooth local or global support representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Fréchet–Regular Coincidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminological coincidence under the standard finite-dimensional lower-subdifferential convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\). When the Fréchet and regular lower subdifferentials are both defined by the first-order condition
\[
\liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{f(x)-f(\bar x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\ge 0,
\]
they coincide:
\[
\widehat\partial_F f(\bar x)=\widehat\partial f(\bar x).
\]
Thus “Fréchet” and “regular” name the same lower subdifferential under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite-dimensional variational analysis, the Fréchet and regular lower subdifferentials are the same object when both use the standard first-order lower-approximation convention.
assumptions_latex: Both symbols use the lower first-order quotient convention in Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_F f(\bar x)=\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\).

Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) with \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and let \(\widehat N\) denote the Fréchet regular normal cone. Then
\[
v\in\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v,-1)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{epi}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x)).
\]
Consequently, regular subgradients are exactly the horizontal components of regular epigraph normals whose vertical component is normalized to \(-1\). This identifies first-order lower support of \(f\) with regular normal geometry of its epigraph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional lower-Hadamard directional characterization and resulting convex geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\), and define
\[
df(\bar x)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)}{t}.
\]
Then
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,w\rangle\le df(\bar x)(w)\ \text{for every }w\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\}.
\]
Consequently, \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, possibly empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Regular subgradients are exactly the linear functionals dominated in every direction by the lower Hadamard directional derivative; consequently the regular subdifferential is closed and convex, though it may be empty.
assumptions_latex: \(df(\bar x)\) denotes the lower Hadamard directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)=\{v:\langle v,w\rangle\le df(\bar x)(w)\ \forall w\}\), and this set is closed and convex.

notation.meaning: lower Hadamard directional derivative of f at the reference point in direction w

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(\varepsilon\ge0\), define
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n\mid \liminf_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\ne\bar x}}\frac{f(x)-f(\bar x)-\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\ge-\varepsilon\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) when \(f(x)\ge f(\bar x)+\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle-(\varepsilon+o(1))\|x-\bar x\|\) as \(x\to\bar x\). For \(\varepsilon=0\), this reduces to the Fréchet subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epsilon-subgradient is a Fréchet subgradient whose local first-order support inequality may lose epsilon times the displacement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Tolerance Is Not a Minkowski Enlargement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Downward cusp showing that positive tolerance can create approximate regular subgradients even when the exact regular subdifferential is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x)=-|x|\) at \(0\),
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(0)=
\begin{cases}
\varnothing,&0\le\varepsilon<1,\\
[1-\varepsilon,\,\varepsilon-1],&\varepsilon\ge1.
\end{cases}
\]
In particular, \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\), whereas \(\widehat\partial_1f(0)=\{0\}\). Hence, in general,
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\ne\widehat\partial f(\bar x)+\varepsilon\mathbb B.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the downward cusp the exact regular subdifferential is empty, but sufficiently large tolerance produces epsilon-subgradients. Thus the epsilon-subdifferential is not generally an epsilon-ball enlargement of the exact regular subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(0)=\varnothing\) for \(\varepsilon<1\) and \([1-\varepsilon,\varepsilon-1]\) for \(\varepsilon\ge1\); hence the Minkowski-enlargement formula fails in general.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Tolerance Is Not a Minkowski Enlargement

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometry and Monotonicity of Fréchet Epsilon-Subdifferentials
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structural properties of the tolerance-indexed family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\). For every \(\varepsilon\ge0\),
\[
\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)=\left\{v:\langle v,w\rangle\le df(\bar x)(w)+\varepsilon\|w\|\ \text{for all }w\in\mathbb{R}^n\right\},
\]
where \(df\) is the lower Hadamard directional derivative. Thus every \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, and
\[
0\le\varepsilon_1\le\varepsilon_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f(\bar x)\subseteq\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epsilon-subdifferential consists of linear functionals dominated by the lower directional derivative up to epsilon times direction length. Its values are closed, convex, and nested as epsilon increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(\widehat\partial_\varepsilon f(\bar x)\) is closed and convex, and \(\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_1}f(\bar x)\subseteq\widehat\partial_{\varepsilon_2}f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Geometry and Monotonicity of Fréchet Epsilon-Subdifferentials

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Indicator and Distance Representations of Limiting Normal Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expresses limiting normal cones through limiting subdifferentials of the indicator and distance functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^k\) be closed, let \(\bar x\in C\), and let \(B:=\{v\in\mathbb R^k:\lVert v\rVert\le1\}\). Define \(\Psi_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\Psi_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise, and define \(d_C(x):=\inf_{y\in C}\lVert x-y\rVert\). Then \[N_C(\bar x)=\partial\Psi_C(\bar x),\qquad N_C(\bar x)\cap B=\partial d_C(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a closed set, the limiting normal cone equals the limiting subdifferential of the set's indicator function, while its unit-bounded part equals the limiting subdifferential of the distance function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_C(\bar x)=\partial\Psi_C(\bar x),\qquad N_C(\bar x)\cap B=\partial d_C(\bar x)

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 Basic Definitions and Representations p. 40

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the Mordukhovich, or basic, subdifferential is
\[
\partial_M f(\bar x):=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\f(x)\to f(\bar x)}}\widehat\partial f(x).
\]
Thus \(v\in\partial_M f(\bar x)\) precisely when sequences \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(v_k\to v\) exist such that \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\) and \(v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\) for all \(k\). The construction retains nonconvex first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Mordukhovich subdifferential is the unconvexified outer limit of nearby regular subdifferentials under function-value convergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Mordukhovich Subdifferential

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(\bar x\). Under the standard finite-dimensional definitions, the limiting subdifferential and the Mordukhovich basic subdifferential coincide:
\[
\partial_L f(\bar x)=\partial_M f(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\f(x)\to f(\bar x)}}\widehat\partial f(x).
\]
Both sides therefore consist of exactly the strong limits \(v_k\to v\) of regular subgradients \(v_k\in\widehat\partial f(x_k)\) along sequences satisfying \(x_k\to\bar x\) and \(f(x_k)\to f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, “limiting” and “Mordukhovich basic” denote the same unconvexified sequential subdifferential.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Subgradient Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete one-dimensional illustration of unconvexified limiting structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) finite at \(\bar x\), the regular and Mordukhovich subdifferentials satisfy
\[
\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_M f(\bar x).
\]
The inclusion can be strict, and the Mordukhovich subdifferential need not be convex. For the locally Lipschitz function \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x)=-|x|\),
\[
\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing,\qquad \partial_M f(0)=\{-1,1\}.
\]
This example displays the unconvexified structure of the basic limiting construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular subdifferential is contained in the limiting one, but the inclusion can be strict and the limiting set can be nonconvex; for minus absolute value at zero it is the two-point set consisting of minus one and one.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb{R}\) for the general inclusion.
For the example, \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is defined by \(f(x)=-|x|\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\partial f(\bar x)\subseteq\partial_M f(\bar x)\), and for \(f(x)=-|x|\), \(\widehat\partial f(0)=\varnothing\) while \(\partial_M f(0)=\{-1,1\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional locally Lipschitz definition and limiting-subgradient representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Clarke subdifferential of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
\partial^C f(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,d\rangle\leq f^\circ(\bar x;d)\ \text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n\},
\]
where
\[
f^\circ(\bar x;d):=\limsup_{x\to\bar x,\,t\downarrow0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t}.
\]
For locally Lipschitz \(f\), the set \(\partial^C f(\bar x)\) is nonempty, compact, and convex, and
\[
\partial^C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\partial f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential consists of the vectors dominated by the Clarke generalized directional derivative. For a locally Lipschitz function, it is a nonempty compact convex set equal to the closed convex hull of the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^C f(\bar x)\) is a nonempty compact convex set and equals \(\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}\partial f(\bar x)\).

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Subdifferentials and Regularity p. 170

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual equivalence between the Clarke generalized directional derivative and Clarke subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\),
\[
f^\circ(\bar x;d)=\max_{v\in\partial^C f(\bar x)}\langle v,d\rangle
=\sigma_{\partial^C f(\bar x)}(d).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke generalized directional derivative is the support function of the Clarke subdifferential.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\circ(\bar x;d)=\sigma_{\partial^C f(\bar x)}(d)\) for every \(d\).
knowledge_statements.title: Support-Function Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stability of the finite-dimensional Clarke-subdifferential mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(L<\infty\) such that
\[
\partial^C f(x)\subseteq L\mathbb B\quad(x\in U).
\]
If \(x_k\to x\in U\), \(v_k\to v\), and \(v_k\in\partial^C f(x_k)\), then \(v\in\partial^C f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a locally Lipschitz point, Clarke subgradients are uniformly bounded and the Clarke-subdifferential mapping is upper semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(x\mapsto\partial^C f(x)\) is locally bounded and upper semicontinuous near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Upper Semicontinuity and Local Boundedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional representation through gradients at nearby differentiability points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D_f\) be the differentiability set of \(f\) and
\[
G_f(\bar x):=\left\{\lim_{k\to\infty}\nabla f(x_k):x_k\to\bar x,\ x_k\in D_f\right\}.
\]
Then
\[
\partial^C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}G_f(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke subdifferential is the closed convex hull of limits of gradients at nearby differentiability points.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^C f(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}G_f(\bar x)\).
