assumptions_latex: \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\) is open, \(F:U\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuous, and \(\bar x\in U\).
Near \(\bar x\), finitely many \(C^1\) mappings \(F_i:U\to\mathbb R^m\) satisfy \(F(x)\in\{F_1(x),\ldots,F_p(x)\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(\bar x)\) is the family of Jacobians of the active smooth selections; under the stated derivative-realizability conditions, it equals \(\partial_BF(\bar x)\), and its convex hull equals \(\partial_CF(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional continuous piecewise-\(C^1\) selection model; the generalized-Jacobian identities require explicit realization by classical derivatives.

source_refs.locator: 7.2.1 Piecewise smooth functions p. 656
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
I(\bar x):=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:F(\bar x)=F_i(\bar x)\},\qquad
\mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(\bar x):=\{\nabla F_i(\bar x):i\in I(\bar x)\}.
\]
This is the piecewise-smooth Jacobian model at \(\bar x\). Suppose additionally that, at every differentiability point \(z\) of \(F\) sufficiently near \(\bar x\), one has \(DF(z)=\nabla F_i(z)\) for some \(i\in I(z)\), and that for every \(i\in I(\bar x)\) there are differentiability points \(z_k\to\bar x\) satisfying \(DF(z_k)=\nabla F_i(z_k)\). Then
\[
\partial_BF(\bar x)=\mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(\bar x),
\qquad
\partial_CF(\bar x)=\operatorname{co}\mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The piecewise-smooth Jacobian model collects the Jacobians of active smooth selections. If classical derivatives near the base point come from active selections and every active-selection Jacobian is realized by such derivatives, the model is the Bouligand Jacobian and its convex hull is the Clarke Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Smooth Jacobian Models

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2.1 Piecewise smooth functions p. 656
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Active Pieces Need Not Be Realized
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of equality with the Bouligand Jacobian when an incident smooth piece is never selected nearby.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)\equiv0\), \(F_1(x)\equiv0\), and \(F_2(x)=x\). Then \(F(x)\in\{F_1(x),F_2(x)\}\) and
\[
I(0)=\{1,2\},\qquad \mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(0)=\{0,1\},
\]
but
\[
\partial_BF(0)=\{0\}.
\]
Thus an active-selection family can strictly overestimate the Bouligand Jacobian unless active derivatives are realized along differentiability points of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth piece that merely meets the selected mapping at the reference point can add a spurious active Jacobian if that piece is never selected nearby.
assumptions_latex: \(F,F_1,F_2:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) are defined by \(F=F_1=0\) and \(F_2(x)=x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial_BF(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq\{0,1\}=\mathcal J_{\mathrm{PS}}F(0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Active Pieces Need Not Be Realized

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite continuous selections from finitely many continuous smooth pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With \(I(x):=\{i:F(x)=F_i(x)\}\), for every \(\bar x\) there is a neighborhood \(V\) such that
\[
I(x)\subseteq I(\bar x)\qquad(x\in V).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Only pieces active at the reference point can remain active arbitrarily nearby.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)\subseteq I(\bar x)\) for all \(x\) sufficiently near \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Indices of selections agreeing with the selected mapping at x.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Stability of Active Selections

children.title: Semismoothness
children.top_down_role: Generalized-Jacobian regularity for nonsmooth local modeling.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized-Jacobian linearization error is \(o(\|h\|)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite-dimensional Clarke-Jacobian definition.

source_refs.locator: 7.2.1 Piecewise smooth functions p. 656
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there and
\[
\lim_{\substack{h\to0\\h\ne0}}\ \sup_{V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)}
\frac{\|F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\|}{\|h\|}=0.
\]
Equivalently, for every sequence \(h_k\to0\) with \(h_k\ne0\) and every choice \(V_k\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h_k)\), one has \(F(\bar x+h_k)-F(\bar x)-V_kh_k=o(\|h_k\|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz, directionally differentiable mapping is semismooth when every nearby Clarke-Jacobian linearization has error smaller than first order.
knowledge_statements.title: Semismoothness

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2.1 Piecewise smooth functions p. 656
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic finite-dimensional closure rules for ordinary semismooth mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) and \(G\) be locally Lipschitz and semismooth at \(\bar x\), and let \(H\) be locally Lipschitz and semismooth at \(F(\bar x)\). Whenever dimensionally defined, \(F+G\), \((F,G)\), and \(H\circ F\) are semismooth at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite sums, Cartesian products, and conformable compositions preserve semismoothness.
assumptions_latex: \(F,G\) are locally Lipschitz and semismooth at \(\bar x\).
\(H\) is locally Lipschitz and semismooth at \(F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F+G\), \((F,G)\), and \(H\circ F\) are semismooth at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.title: Semismoothness Closure Calculus

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional piecewise-C1 sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that near \(\bar x\), the locally Lipschitz mapping \(F\) is a continuous selection of finitely many \(C^1\) mappings \(F_1,\ldots,F_q\): \[F(x)\in\{F_1(x),\ldots,F_q(x)\}.\] Then \(F\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\). In particular, locally Lipschitz piecewise-affine mappings are semismooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite piecewise-C1 locally Lipschitz mappings, including piecewise-affine mappings, are semismooth.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
Near \(\bar x\), \(F\) is a continuous selection of finitely many \(C^1\) mappings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is semismooth at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: Finite family of C1 selection functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Smooth Semismoothness

children.title: Strong Semismoothness
children.top_down_role: Strengthened semismooth approximation behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The generalized-Jacobian linearization error is \(O(\|h\|^2)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic-residual version of strong semismoothness.

source_refs.locator: 7.2.1 Piecewise smooth functions p. 656
source_refs.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\) if it is directionally differentiable there and there exist \(c\ge0\) and \(\delta>0\) such that, for every \(h\) with \(0<\|h\|<\delta\) and every \(V\in\partial_C F(\bar x+h)\),
\[
\|F(\bar x+h)-F(\bar x)-Vh\|\le c\|h\|^2.
\]
Thus strong semismoothness implies semismoothness at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong semismoothness requires all nearby generalized-Jacobian linearizations to have uniformly quadratic error, and therefore implies ordinary semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.title: Strong Semismoothness

source_witnesses.locator: 7.2.1 Piecewise smooth functions p. 656
source_witnesses.source_title: Finite-Dimensional Variational Inequalities and Complementarity Problems, Vol. II

assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is continuous and locally represented by finitely many \(C^1\) selection functions near \(\bar x\).
The Jacobian of every local selection is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(F\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\); in particular, every continuous piecewise-affine mapping is strongly semismooth.

notation.meaning: Finite family of local smooth selection functions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sufficient class based on finitely many locally \(C^{1,1}\) selections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If locally \(F(x)\in\{F_1(x),\ldots,F_N(x)\}\) for finitely many \(C^1\) selections with locally Lipschitz Jacobians, then \(F\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\). Continuous piecewise-affine mappings form a special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous finite piecewise-smooth mapping with locally Lipschitz selection Jacobians is strongly semismooth; continuous piecewise-affine mappings are the basic special case.
knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Smooth Sufficient Classes

assumptions_latex: \(F\) and \(G\) are compatible finite-dimensional mappings strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\).
For composition, \(H\) is strongly semismooth at \(F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite linear combinations of \(F\) and \(G\), and the composition \(H\circ F\), are strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic closure properties for locally Lipschitz strongly semismooth mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scalars \(a,b\), \(aF+bG\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\). If \(F\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\) and \(H\) is strongly semismooth at \(F(\bar x)\), then \(H\circ F\) is strongly semismooth at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong semismoothness is preserved by finite linear combinations and compatible finite-dimensional compositions.
knowledge_statements.title: Closure of Strong Semismoothness

children.title: Semismoothness Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Mapping irregularities that invalidate semismooth local models.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(t)=t^2\sin(1/t)\) for \(t\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mapping \(f\) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable at \(0\), but is not semismooth there.

notation.meaning: Clarke generalized Jacobian of the scalar mapping

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar counterexample showing that local Lipschitz continuity and directional differentiability do not imply semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(t)=t^2\sin(1/t)\) when \(t\ne0\), one has \(f'(0;d)=0\) for every \(d\), but the residuals \(f(t)-f(0)-Vt\), with \(V\in\partial_Cf(t)\), are not \(o(|t|)\) uniformly as \(t\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function t squared times sin(1/t) is locally Lipschitz and directionally differentiable at zero, yet its nearby generalized-Jacobian models retain a first-order oscillatory error.
knowledge_statements.title: Directional Differentiability Is Not Sufficient

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz Continuity Does Not Ensure Directional Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A distinct oscillatory failure mechanism in which a locally Lipschitz scalar mapping lacks the directional derivative required for semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(h(0)=0\) and, for \(t\ne0\),
\[
h(t)=\int_0^t \sin\!\left(\log\frac1{|s|}\right)\,ds.
\]
Then \(h\) is locally Lipschitz, while the quotient \(h(t)/t\) has no limit as \(t\downarrow0\). Consequently \(h'(0;1)\) does not exist and \(h\) is not semismooth at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral of a bounded logarithmically oscillating function is locally Lipschitz but has no directional derivative at zero, so it cannot be semismooth there.
assumptions_latex: \(h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(h(0)=0\) and \(h(t)=\int_0^t\sin(\log(1/|s|))\,ds\) for \(t\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is locally Lipschitz at \(0\), but \(h'(0;1)\) does not exist; hence \(h\) is not semismooth at \(0\).

notation.meaning: One-sided directional derivative of h at zero in direction one

knowledge_statements.title: Local Lipschitz Continuity Does Not Ensure Directional Differentiability

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) is defined by \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(t)=t\sin(\log|t|)\) for \(t\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local Lipschitz continuity alone does not ensure semismoothness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by persistent directional oscillation at the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is locally Lipschitz at \(0\): away from \(0\), its derivative is \(f'(t)=\sin(\log|t|)+\cos(\log|t|)\), which is bounded. Nevertheless,
\[
\frac{f(t)-f(0)}{t}=\sin(\log|t|)
\]
has no limit as \(t\downarrow0\). Hence the directional derivative \(f'(0;1)\) does not exist, so \(f\) is not semismooth at \(0\). This identifies directional differentiability as a genuine boundary not supplied by local Lipschitz continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The locally Lipschitz function t sin(log|t|) oscillates too strongly to possess a directional derivative at zero and hence is not semismooth there.
knowledge_statements.title: Semismoothness Failure Boundary

children.title: Regular Coderivative
children.top_down_role: Coderivative generated by regular graph normals.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\) is obtained by slicing the regular normal cone to \(\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Fréchet-normal coderivative.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(y^*\in Y\), the regular coderivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is the set-valued mapping
\[
\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*\in X:(x^*,-y^*)\in\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
The minus sign in the output-dual component is part of the coderivative convention. If \((\bar x,\bar y)\notin\operatorname{gph}F\), the regular coderivative is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regular coderivative consists of input covectors whose pairing with the negative output covector is a regular normal to the mapping's graph.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular Coderivative

children.title: Limiting Coderivative
children.top_down_role: Coderivative generated by limiting graph normals.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\) is obtained by slicing the limiting normal cone to \(\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Mordukhovich coderivative.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(y^*\in Y\), the limiting coderivative of \(F\) at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) is
\[
D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*\in X:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Here \(N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\) is the outer limit of regular graph normals at nearby graph points. Consequently, \(\widehat D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting coderivative slices the limiting normal cone to the graph and contains the corresponding regular coderivative values.
knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Coderivative

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting Coderivative and Smooth Single-Valued Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limiting coderivative defined by normal geometry of a locally closed graph, with its positive homogeneity and smooth reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\), let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and suppose \(\operatorname{gph}F\) is locally closed around \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Define
\[D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(w):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:(v,-w)\in N\big((\bar x,\bar y);\operatorname{gph}F\big)\right\},\qquad w\in\mathbb R^m.\]
This is a positively homogeneous mapping from \(\mathbb R^m\) to subsets of \(\mathbb R^n\). If \(F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) is smooth around \(\bar x\) and \(\bar y=F(\bar x)\), then
\[D^*F(\bar x)(w)=\{\nabla F(\bar x)^*w\}\qquad\forall w\in\mathbb R^m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The limiting coderivative is obtained by taking signed slices of the limiting normal cone to a mapping's graph. It is positively homogeneous and reduces to the adjoint Jacobian for a smooth single-valued mapping.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}F\text{ is locally closed around }(\bar x,\bar y)
F\text{ is single-valued and smooth around }\bar x\text{ for the Jacobian reduction}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(w)=\{v:(v,-w)\in N((\bar x,\bar y);\operatorname{gph}F)\},\qquad D^*F(\bar x)(w)=\{\nabla F(\bar x)^*w\}\text{ in the smooth single-valued case}

children.title: Clarke Coderivative
children.top_down_role: Convexified coderivative regime.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_C^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\) uses the closed convex hull of limiting graph normals.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convexified-normal coderivative.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the Clarke normal cone by
\[
N_C^C(\bar x,\bar y):=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}N_C(\bar x,\bar y),
\]
where \(C:=\operatorname{gph}F\). For \(y^*\in Y\), the Clarke coderivative is
\[
D_C^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*):=\{x^*\in X:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{
\operatorname{gph}F}^C(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Thus it convexifies graph-normal directions before taking the coderivative slice; it need not equal the pointwise convex hull of \(D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke coderivative slices the closed convex hull of limiting normals to the graph; convexification occurs before fixing the output covector.
knowledge_statements.title: Clarke Coderivative

source_witnesses.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

children.top_down_role: Infinite-dimensional coderivative variants distinguished by weak-star and strong convergence behavior.

children.title: Mixed Coderivatives
children.top_down_role: Coderivative geometry combining distinct convergence modes across primal and dual components.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Asplund spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
The sequential mixed outer limit below is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mixed coderivative enforces norm convergence in the output-dual component and weak-star convergence in the input-dual component.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Asplund-space mixed coderivative.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.1 Lipschitzian Properties via Normal and Mixed Coderivatives p. 385
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(y^*\in Y^*\), one has \(x^*\in D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\) when there exist \((x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y)\) in \(\operatorname{gph}F\), \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), and
\[
(x_k^*,-y_k^*)\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}(\operatorname{gph}F;x_k,y_k)
\]
such that \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}x^*\) while \(y_k^*\to y^*\) in norm. The asymmetric convergence requirements distinguish the mixed coderivative from the normal coderivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mixed coderivative takes limits of approximate regular graph normals, using weak-star convergence for input covectors but norm convergence for output covectors.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Coderivatives

children.title: Normal Coderivatives
children.top_down_role: Coderivative geometry based on the corresponding normal convergence regime.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Asplund spaces, \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\), and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
The sequential normal outer limit below is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The normal coderivative permits weak-star convergence in both dual components.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential Asplund-space normal coderivative.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.1 Lipschitzian Properties via Normal and Mixed Coderivatives p. 385

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(y^*\in Y^*\), one has \(x^*\in D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\) when there exist \((x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y)\) in \(\operatorname{gph}F\), \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), and
\[
(x_k^*,-y_k^*)\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}(\operatorname{gph}F;x_k,y_k)
\]
such that \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}x^*\) and \(y_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}y^*\). Thus both dual components use weak-star convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal coderivative takes limits of approximate regular graph normals while allowing weak-star convergence in both dual components.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal Coderivatives

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A normal-coderivative domain condition yields minimization of the associated dual functional over the reference value set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:X\rightrightarrows Y be inner semicontinuous at \bar x\in\operatorname{dom}F and convex-valued around \bar x. If \bar y\in F(\bar x) and y^*\in\operatorname{dom}D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y), then \langle y^*,\bar y\rangle=\min_{y\in F(\bar x)}\langle y^*,y\rangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a multifunction is inner semicontinuous at the reference point and convex-valued nearby, normal-coderivative activity at a graph point forces that output point to minimize the corresponding dual linear functional over the value set at the reference point.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is inner semicontinuous at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle y^*,\bar y\rangle=\min_{y\in F(\bar x)}\langle y^*,y\rangle.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex graph structure yields graphical N-regularity and a global supporting-functional representation of the normal and mixed coderivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:X\rightrightarrows Y have a convex graph. For every (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F and y^*\in Y^*, F is N\text{-regular at }(\bar x,\bar y), and D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=\left\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,\bar x\rangle-\langle y^*,\bar y\rangle=\max_{(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F}\left[\langle x^*,x\rangle-\langle y^*,y\rangle\right]\right\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multifunction with a convex graph is graphically N-regular at every graph point. Its normal and mixed coderivatives coincide and consist exactly of the input covectors whose associated linear functional is maximized over the graph at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is N-regular at }(\bar x,\bar y),\quad D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=\left\{x^*\in X^*\mid \langle x^*,\bar x\rangle-\langle y^*,\bar y\rangle=\max_{(x,y)\in\operatorname{gph}F}[\langle x^*,x\rangle-\langle y^*,y\rangle]\right\}.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)=D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\).

source_refs.locator: 4.2.1 Lipschitzian Properties via Normal and Mixed Coderivatives p. 385

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In finite-dimensional dual spaces, weak-star convergence and norm convergence coincide. Therefore the defining convergence requirements for the mixed and normal coderivatives are identical, and for every \(y^*\in Y^*\),
\[
D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*).
\]
The equality concerns the entire set-valued coderivative mappings, not merely their values at \(y^*=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, weak-star and norm convergence agree, so mixed and normal coderivatives coincide at every output covector.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixed–Normal Coincidence

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2.1 Lipschitzian Properties via Normal and Mixed Coderivatives p. 385

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coincidence under norm precompactness of output-dual sequences admissible in the normal-coderivative construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(y^*\in Y^*\). Suppose every sequence \((y_k^*)\) occurring in a defining normal-coderivative sequence with \(y_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}y^*\) has a subsequence converging to \(y^*\) in norm. Then
\[
D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*).
\]
If this condition holds for every \(y^*\), the two coderivative mappings coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed and normal coderivatives coincide whenever the admissible weak-star-convergent output covectors are sequentially norm precompact; finite dimensionality is a special case.
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are Asplund spaces and the sequential mixed and normal coderivatives use the conventions of the sibling definition leaves.
Every admissible output-dual sequence weak-star converging to the selected \(y^*\) has a norm-convergent subsequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)=D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Output-Dual Compactness Coincidence

children.title: Convergence-Mode Gap
children.top_down_role: Infinite-dimensional settings where weak-star and strong behavior separate the variants.

assumptions_latex: Mixed and normal coderivatives are defined by the stated sequential convergence modes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\), with possible strict inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional gap caused by weak-star versus norm convergence.

source_refs.locator: 4.2.1 Lipschitzian Properties via Normal and Mixed Coderivatives p. 385

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Norm convergence of \(y_k^*\) implies weak-star convergence, so for every \(y^*\in Y^*\),
\[
D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\subset D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*).
\]
In infinite-dimensional spaces the converse can fail because a weak-star convergent sequence of output covectors need not converge in norm. A normal-coderivative element represented only by such a sequence may therefore be excluded from the mixed coderivative. Finite dimensionality removes this gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mixed coderivative is contained in the normal coderivative; infinite-dimensional weak-star convergence without norm convergence can make the containment strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Convergence-Mode Gap

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit infinite-dimensional strict inclusion generated by a weakly null but non-norm-null orthonormal sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The resulting mapping \(f:\mathbb R\to\ell^2\) is locally Lipschitz and satisfies
\[
1\in D_N^*f(0,0)(0),\qquad D_M^*f(0,0)(0)=\{0\}.
\]
Thus the inclusion \(D_M^*f(0,0)(0)\subset D_N^*f(0,0)(0)\) is strict.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally Lipschitz mapping into ell-two converts weakly null orthonormal directions into a nonzero normal-coderivative value at zero, while its mixed coderivative at zero remains trivial.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\in C_c^1((-1,1))\) satisfies \(\phi(0)=0\) and \(\phi'(0)=1\), and the intervals \((x_n-a_n,x_n+a_n)\) are pairwise disjoint.
Define \(f(t)=a_n\phi((t-x_n)/a_n)e_n\) on the \(n\)-th interval and \(f(t)=0\) elsewhere.

children.title: Graph-Normal Representation
children.top_down_role: Direct realization of coderivatives through graph normals.

assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces and \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\).
\(N^\diamond\) denotes the regular, limiting, or Clarke normal cone, with the matching coderivative \(D_\diamond^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Coderivative values are exactly signed slices of the corresponding graph-normal cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified finite-dimensional representation for three basic coderivatives.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Generalized Differentiation in Banach Spaces p. 3
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y^*\in Y\), the graph-normal representation is
\[
D_\diamond^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
=\{x^*\in X:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}^\diamond(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\operatorname{gph}D_\diamond^*F(\bar x,\bar y)
=\{(y^*,x^*):(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}F}^\diamond(\bar x,\bar y)\}.
\]
Choosing \(\diamond\) as regular, limiting, or Clarke gives the corresponding coderivative without changing the sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each basic coderivative is exactly a signed slice of the matching normal cone to the graph, equivalently a coordinate-swapped graph-normal relation.

children.title: Single-Valued Mapping Reductions
children.top_down_role: Coderivative reductions for smooth, Lipschitz, and piecewise-smooth mappings.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Valued Mapping Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-coderivative reduction, including the exact strictly differentiable case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y^*\in Y\), regard the single-valued mapping as \(x\mapsto\{f(x)\}\). Its limiting coderivative is
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\big\{x^*\in X:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\big\}.
\]
If \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\), then
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)^T y^*\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-valued coderivative is obtained from normals to the mapping's graph; strict differentiability reduces it to the transpose derivative applied to the dual argument.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb{R}^n\), \(Y=\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(f:X\to Y\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\).
The coderivative and normal cone are the limiting Mordukhovich constructions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\{x^*:(x^*,-y^*)\in N_{\operatorname{gph}f}(\bar x,f(\bar x))\}\), with \(D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\{\nabla f(\bar x)^T y^*\}\) when \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional norm bound for a locally Lipschitz single-valued mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) with constant \(L\). Then, for every \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\) and every \(x^*\in D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)\),
\[
\|x^*\|\le L\|y^*\|.
\]
Consequently, \(D^*f(\bar x)(0)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local Lipschitz constant bounds every coderivative output by that constant times the dual argument norm; in particular, the coderivative at the zero dual argument is zero.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) is single-valued and Lipschitz on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\) with constant \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)\Longrightarrow \|x^*\|\le L\|y^*\|,\qquad D^*f(\bar x)(0)=\{0\}.

notation.meaning: A local Lipschitz constant for f

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Coderivative Norm Bound

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coderivative upper representation for a finite piecewise-C1 mapping, retaining normals to branch domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that near \(\bar x\),
\[
\operatorname{gph}f=\bigcup_{i=1}^r\{(x,f_i(x)):x\in\Omega_i\},
\]
where each \(\Omega_i\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is locally closed, each \(f_i\) is \(C^1\) near \(\bar x\), and \(f=f_i\) on \(\Omega_i\). With \(I(\bar x):=\{i:\bar x\in\Omega_i\}\), for every \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\),
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)
\subset
\bigcup_{i\in I(\bar x)}
\left(\nabla f_i(\bar x)^Ty^*+N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\right).
\]
The branch-domain normal terms cannot generally be omitted at junctions or boundaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every coderivative value of a finite piecewise-smooth mapping lies in an active branch Jacobian-transpose value plus a normal to that branch domain; the domain normals retain junction effects.
assumptions_latex: The displayed finite graph decomposition holds locally at \((\bar x,f(\bar x))\).
Each \(\Omega_i\) is locally closed, and each \(f_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
Coderivatives and branch-domain normals are limiting constructions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)\subset\bigcup_{i\in I(\bar x)}\left(\nabla f_i(\bar x)^Ty^*+N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\right).

notation.meaning: Indices of branch domains active at the reference point
Limiting normal cone to the ith branch domain

children.title: Inverse-Mapping Representation

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Mapping Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-transposition identity for limiting coderivatives in finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). Since \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}\) is obtained from \(\operatorname{gph}F\) by interchanging coordinates, for every \(x^*\in X\) and \(y^*\in Y\),
\[
y^*\in D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)(x^*)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
-x^*\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(-y^*).
\]
Equivalently, \((y^*,-x^*)\) is normal to \(\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}\) exactly when \((-x^*,y^*)\) is normal to \(\operatorname{gph}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Swapping a mapping's graph coordinates swaps the dual coordinates and signs, yielding an exact coderivative identity between the mapping and its inverse.
assumptions_latex: \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and the graph is locally closed at \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
Coderivatives use the same limiting normal-cone convention for \(F\) and \(F^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y^*\in D^*F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)(x^*)\iff -x^*\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(-y^*)\).

notation.meaning: Limiting coderivative of F at a graph point

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\), define the scalar function \(\varphi_{y^*}:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(\varphi_{y^*}(x)=\langle y^*,f(x)\rangle\). Then
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)
=\partial\varphi_{y^*}(\bar x)
=\{\nabla f(\bar x)^Ty^*\}.
\]
Thus scalar differentiation and graph-normal coderivation give the same covector, with no convexification or closure required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth mapping, scalarizing by a dual vector and differentiating gives exactly the coderivative: the transpose Jacobian times that vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:X\to Y\) is strictly Lipschitzian at \(\bar x\), then for every \(y^*\in Y^*\) its limiting coderivative is recovered by the limiting subdifferential of the scalarization:
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)
=\partial\big(x\mapsto\langle y^*,f(x)\rangle\big)(\bar x).
\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f(x)=|x|\) and scalarize with \(y^*=-1\). The limiting graph normals arising from the two smooth branches give
\[
D^*f(0)(-1)=\{-1,1\}.
\]
By contrast, Clarke scalarization convexifies the branch information:
\[
\partial_C\langle-1,f\rangle(0)=\partial_C(-|\cdot|)(0)=[-1,1].
\]
Hence a convexified scalar subdifferential can strictly overestimate the limiting coderivative and cannot generally serve as an exact replacement for it.

knowledge_statements.title: Graphical Derivative–Coderivative Polarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact tangent-normal polarity for a locally convex graph in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Local convexity gives the tangent-normal polarity
\[
N_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)
=T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)^\circ.
\]
Since \(v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\) exactly when \((u,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\), for every \(x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(y^*\in\mathbb{R}^m\),
\[
x^*\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\langle x^*,u\rangle-\langle y^*,v\rangle\le 0
\quad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ and every }v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a locally convex graph, coderivative membership is equivalent to the polar inequality for every direction pair belonging to the graphical derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\), \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and the graph is locally closed and convex near \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
The graphical derivative uses the contingent tangent cone, and the coderivative uses the limiting normal cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^*\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)\iff \langle x^*,u\rangle-\langle y^*,v\rangle\le 0\) for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and every \(v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)\).

If the graph is normally regular at \((\bar x,\bar y)\), so that \(\widehat N_{\operatorname{gph}F}=N_{\operatorname{gph}F}\) there, the same equivalence holds with \(D^*F\) in place of \(\widehat D^*F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarizing the graphical derivative always recovers the regular coderivative; it also recovers the limiting coderivative when the graph is normally regular.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic properties and polarity of graphical derivatives and coderivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive homogeneity, regular-to-limiting inclusions, and primal-dual polarity at a graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m, \bar x\in\operatorname{dom}S, and \bar u\in S(\bar x). Then DS(\bar x\mid\bar u),\widehat DS(\bar x\mid\bar u),D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u), and \widehat D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u) are outer semicontinuous and positively homogeneous. The regular mappings are graph-convex, hence sublinear, and
\widehat DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w)\subset DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w),\qquad \widehat D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y)\subset D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y).
If \operatorname{gph}S is locally closed at (\bar x,\bar u)—in particular, if S is outer semicontinuous—then
v\in\widehat D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y)\iff \langle v,w\rangle\leq\langle y,z\rangle\quad\text{for every }w\text{ and every }z\in DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w),
and
z\in\widehat DS(\bar x\mid\bar u)(w)\iff \langle v,w\rangle\leq\langle y,z\rangle\quad\text{for every }y\text{ and every }v\in D^*S(\bar x\mid\bar u)(y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All four graphical derivative and coderivative mappings are outer semicontinuous and positively homogeneous. The regular variants are graph-convex and are contained in their limiting counterparts. If the graph is locally closed at the reference point, membership in either regular object is equivalent to the stated pairing inequality against every element of the opposite limiting object.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}S\text{ is locally closed at }(\bar x,\bar u)\text{ for the polarity equivalences}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: DS,\widehat DS,D^*S,\widehat D^*S\text{ are outer semicontinuous and positively homogeneous};\quad \widehat DS\subset DS,\ \widehat D^*S\subset D^*S;\quad \text{under local closedness, the stated polarity equivalences hold.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is strictly differentiable at \(\bar x\) with derivative \(A\), then its primal generalized derivative agrees with the classical derivative:
\[
Df(\bar x)(u)=\{Au\}\quad\text{for every }u\in X.
\]
Its dual generalized derivative agrees with the classical adjoint:
\[
D^*f(\bar x)(y^*)=\{A^*y^*\}
\quad\text{for every }y^*\in Y.
\]
For a linear mapping, these identities hold at every base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a strictly differentiable mapping, the graphical derivative is the classical derivative and the coderivative is its adjoint.
knowledge_statements.title: Classical Adjoint Consistency

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Adjoint of a bounded linear operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical adjoints between dual normed spaces and the adjoint representation of the scalar-valued chain rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be normed spaces and \(T\in L_C(X,Y)\). There is a unique operator \(T^*\in L_C(Y^*,X^*)\) such that \(\langle T^*y^*,x\rangle=\langle y^*,Tx\rangle\) for every \(x\in X\) and \(y^*\in Y^*\); it is called the adjoint of \(T\). If \(F:X\to Y\) is differentiable at \(x\) and \(\theta:Y\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at \(F(x)\), then \((\theta\circ F)'(x)=F'(x)^*\theta'(F(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded linear operator has a unique adjoint obtained by transposing the dual pairing. This lets the scalar-valued chain rule be written by applying the adjoint derivative of the inner map to the derivative of the outer function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \langle T^*y^*,x\rangle=\langle y^*,Tx\rangle\quad\forall x\in X,\ y^*\in Y^*,\qquad (\theta\circ F)'(x)=F'(x)^*\theta'(F(x))

For \(f(x)=|x|\), the graphical derivative satisfies \(Df(0)(u)=\{|u|\}\). If limiting coderivatives were determined by polarizing this graphical derivative, then for \(y^*=-1\) one would require

x^*u+|u|\le 0\quad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb{R},

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The finite system \(\{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_s\}\) is locally extremal at \(\bar x\) if there exists \(\delta>0\) such that, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there are vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\in X\) satisfying \(\max_i\|a_i\|<\varepsilon\) and

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local extremality of a finite set system
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines local extremality through vanishing translations that locally destroy the common intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let n\ge 2, let \Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n\subset X be nonempty, and let \bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^n\Omega_i. The point \bar x is locally extremal for \{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n\} if there exist a neighborhood U of \bar x and sequences a_{ik}\to0 such that \bigcap_{i=1}^n(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\cap U=\varnothing for all sufficiently large k. The tuple \{\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_n,\bar x\} is then an extremal system. For n=2 this is equivalent to the existence of a neighborhood U of \bar x such that, for every \varepsilon>0, some a\in\varepsilon B satisfies (\Omega_1+a)\cap\Omega_2\cap U=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common point is locally extremal when vanishing translations of the sets eventually eliminate their intersection in a fixed neighborhood. For two sets, every positive translation scale equivalently admits a translation of one set that locally separates the pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar x\text{ is locally extremal}\iff\exists U,\exists a_{ik}\to0:\ \bigcap_{i=1}^n(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\cap U=\varnothing\text{ eventually}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1=\mathbb R\times\{0\}\) and \(\Omega_2=\{(x,x^2(x+1)):x\in\mathbb R\}\). Since \(x^2(x+1)\ge0\) near \(0\), an arbitrarily small upward translation of \(\Omega_2\) separates the sets in a fixed neighborhood of \((0,0)\). Nevertheless, \(x\mapsto x^2(x+1)\) is a surjective cubic, so after arbitrary translations of both sets their intersection condition is \(x^2(x+1)=c\) for some \(c\in\mathbb R\), which always has a solution. Thus the pair is locally extremal at \((0,0)\) but not globally extremal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph of the surjective cubic x²(x+1) lies on one side of the horizontal axis near the origin, permitting local separation, while its full range prevents separation after any global translations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint specialization of a power-rate convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the power-rate convention \(R_\alpha(r):=\gamma r^\alpha\), setting \(\alpha=1\) gives \(R_1(r)=\gamma r\). Consequently, the rated-extremality condition specializes to \[\left(\bigcap_{i=1}^{m}(\Omega_i-a_{ik})\right)\cap B(\bar x,\gamma r_k)=\varnothing,\qquad r_k:=\max_i\|a_{ik}\|\downarrow0,\] which is precisely the linear-rate separation condition. Whether the endpoint \(\alpha=1\) is included in the source definition or treated separately must be fixed by convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a power rate, choosing exponent one makes the localization radius proportional to perturbation size and yields linear extremality.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Rate Specialization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic substitution \(\alpha=1\) is correct, and property is an appropriate content kind for this leaf. However, calling it precisely the linear-extremality specialization depends on the unsupported definitions in the two prerequisite records and on whether the cited theory includes the endpoint.

children.title: Sublinear Rate Boundary
children.top_down_role: Rate regimes where linear extremality no longer captures the local separation behavior.

assumptions_latex: The power localization rate is \(R_\alpha(r)=\gamma r^\alpha\) with \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(0\le\alpha<1\), \(R_\alpha(r)/r\to\infty\); at \(\alpha=1\), the ratio equals \(\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between neighborhoods asymptotically larger than perturbations and neighborhoods of comparable size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(R_\alpha(r):=\gamma r^\alpha\), one has \[\frac{R_\alpha(r)}{r}=\gamma r^{\alpha-1}.\] Hence \(R_\alpha(r)/r\to\infty\) as \(r\downarrow0\) exactly when \(0\le\alpha<1\), whereas \(R_1(r)/r=\gamma\). Thus \(\alpha=1\) is the boundary between sublinear-power localization, whose observation radius dominates the perturbation magnitude, and linear localization, whose two scales remain comparable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Power exponents below one give neighborhoods asymptotically larger than the perturbations; exponent one is the linear boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Sublinear Rate Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ratio calculation is correct, and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. A source is still required to establish that \(0\leq\alpha<1\) is the intended named sublinear regime in this taxonomy rather than merely an algebraic observation under a locally introduced convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact limiting-normal necessity under Asplund, local-closedness, and SNC assumptions, together with the finite-dimensional equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X and \bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2. Suppose \{\Omega_1,\Omega_2\} is linearly subextremal around \bar x, X is Asplund, both sets are locally closed around \bar x, and at least one set is sequentially normally compact at \bar x. Then there exists x^*\in X^* such that
\[
0\neq x^*\in N(\bar x;\Omega_1)\cap\big(-N(\bar x;\Omega_2)\big).
\]
If \dim X<\infty, this nonzero opposite-normal condition is necessary and sufficient for linear subextremality of the two-set system around \bar x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated Asplund, local-closedness, and sequential-normal-compactness assumptions, a linearly subextremal pair has a nonzero limiting normal to one set whose negative is a limiting normal to the other. In finite dimensions, this exact opposite-normal certificate is equivalent to linear subextremality.
assumptions_latex: \Omega_1\text{ and }\Omega_2\text{ are locally closed around }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^*\neq0:\ x^*\in N(\bar x;\Omega_1)\cap[-N(\bar x;\Omega_2)];\qquad \dim X<\infty\Rightarrow\big(\text{linear subextremality}\iff\exists x^*\neq0\text{ satisfying this condition}\big).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way certificate in Banach spaces, its locally closed Asplund-space converse, and the resulting characterization of Asplund spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X, where X is a Banach space, and let \bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2. If for every \varepsilon>0 there exist \widehat x_i\in\Omega_i\cap(\bar x+\varepsilon\mathbb B) and x_i^*\in\widehat N_\varepsilon(\widehat x_i;\Omega_i), i=1,2, such that
\[
\|x_1^*+x_2^*\|\leq\varepsilon,
\qquad \|x_1^*\|+\|x_2^*\|=1,
\]
then \{\Omega_1,\Omega_2\} is linearly subextremal around \bar x. Conversely, if \Omega_1 and \Omega_2 are locally closed, the system is linearly subextremal around \bar x, and X is Asplund, then for every \varepsilon>0 there exist \widehat x_i\in\Omega_i\cap(\bar x+\varepsilon\mathbb B) and x_i^*\in\widehat N(\widehat x_i;\Omega_i) satisfying the same two inequalities. If this converse property holds for every linearly subextremal two-set system in X, then X is Asplund.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily accurate normalized approximate-normal certificates imply linear subextremality. For locally closed sets in an Asplund space, linear subextremality yields normalized Fréchet-normal certificates at nearby points. If that converse is valid for every linearly subextremal pair in a Banach space, the space must be Asplund.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the converse: }\Omega_1,\Omega_2\text{ are locally closed, }\{\Omega_1,\Omega_2\}\text{ is linearly subextremal around }\bar x,\text{ and }X\text{ is Asplund}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \big[\forall\varepsilon>0\text{, the stated normalized }\widehat N_\varepsilon\text{-certificates exist}\big]\Rightarrow\text{linear subextremality};\quad \text{under local closedness and the Asplund hypothesis, linear subextremality yields the stated }\widehat N\text{-certificates}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asplund Characterization by the Approximate Extremal Principle for Multifunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes Asplund spaces through normalized approximate-normal certificates for every closed-valued multifunction extremal system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space. The following are equivalent: (a) \(X\) is Asplund; (b) for every extremal system \(\{S_1,\ldots,S_n,\bar x\}\) at \((\bar s_1,\ldots,\bar s_n)\), with \(S_i:M_i\rightrightarrows X\) closed-valued around \(\bar s_i\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exist \(s_i\in\operatorname{dom}S_i\), \(x_i\in S_i(s_i)\), and \(x_i^*\in X^*\) such that \(d_i(s_i,\bar s_i)\leq\varepsilon\), \(\|x_i-\bar x\|\leq\varepsilon\), \(x_i^*\in\widehat N(x_i;S_i(s_i))+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*\), \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^*=0\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i^*\|=1\); (c) the same assertion holds with \(x_i^*\in\widehat N_\varepsilon(x_i;S_i(s_i))\) replacing the enlarged regular-normal condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Banach space is Asplund exactly when every closed-valued multifunction extremal system admits nearby normalized approximate normals that balance to zero; equivalently, epsilon-normal cones may be used.

\{S_1,\ldots,S_n,\bar x\}\text{ is extremal at }(\bar s_1,\ldots,\bar s_n)
S_i\text{ is closed-valued around }\bar s_i\text{ for every }i
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X\text{ is Asplund}\iff\text{the enlarged regular-normal certificate holds universally}\iff\text{the }\varepsilon\text{-normal certificate holds universally}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient characterization of the approximate extremal principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-function Fréchet-subgradient characterization of approximate extremality in Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space. If the approximate extremal principle holds for every extremal system of two closed sets in \(X\times\mathbb R\), then whenever \((\varphi_1,\varphi_2)\in\mathcal{SL}(\bar x)\), \(\varphi_i:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\), and \(\varphi_1+\varphi_2\) attains a local minimum at \(\bar x\), for every \(\eta>0\) there exist \(x_i\in\bar x+\eta\mathbb B\) such that \(|\varphi_i(x_i)-\varphi_i(\bar x)|\leq\eta\) for \(i=1,2\) and \[0\in\widehat\partial\varphi_1(x_1)+\widehat\partial\varphi_2(x_2)+\eta\mathbb B^*.\] Conversely, if this conclusion holds for every such pair, local minimum, and \(\eta>0\), then the approximate extremal principle holds for every extremal system of two closed sets in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The approximate extremal principle for pairs of closed sets in the product space yields an arbitrarily accurate nearby Fréchet-subgradient balance for semi-Lipschitzian two-function sums. Universal validity of that balance conversely yields the approximate extremal principle for pairs of closed sets in the original space.
assumptions_latex: \varphi_1+\varphi_2\text{ attains a local minimum at }\bar x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x_i\in\bar x+\eta\mathbb B:\ |\varphi_i(x_i)-\varphi_i(\bar x)|\leq\eta\ (i=1,2),\quad 0\in\widehat\partial\varphi_1(x_1)+\widehat\partial\varphi_2(x_2)+\eta\mathbb B^*;\text{ universal validity gives the stated converse extremal principle.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Extremal Principle for Multifunctions and Characterization of Asplund Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives a nontrivial extended-normal balance under ISNC hypotheses and a converse characterization of Asplund spaces using pairs of multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (i) Let \(S_i:M_i\rightrightarrows X\), \(i=1,\ldots,n\), map metric spaces into an Asplund space \(X\). Suppose \(\bar x\) is a local extremal point at \((\bar s_1,\ldots,\bar s_n)\), every \(S_i\) is closed-valued around \(\bar s_i\), and all but at most one \(S_i\) are ISNC at \((\bar s_i,\bar x)\). Then there exist \(x_i^*\in N_+(\bar x;S_i(\bar s_i))\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^n x_i^*=0\) and \((x_1^*,\ldots,x_n^*)\neq0\). (ii) Conversely, if this exact extremal principle holds for every extremal system of two multifunctions into \(X\), with both mappings closed-valued around their reference parameters and at least one mapping ISNC at its reference graph point, then \(X\) is Asplund.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In an Asplund space, a locally extremal closed-valued multifunction system has nontrivial extended normals that sum to zero when all but possibly one mapping are ISNC. Universal validity for qualifying pairs conversely implies that the space is Asplund.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a normal-cone assignment \(N^\circ\) on subsets of a Banach space \(X\). An abstract extremal principle asserts that, whenever a finite locally closed system \(\{\Omega_i\}_{i=1}^m\) is locally extremal at \(\bar x\), for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exist \(x_i\in\Omega_i\cap B(\bar x,\varepsilon)\) and \(x_i^*\in N^\circ_{\Omega_i}(x_i)+\varepsilon B_{X^*}\) such that \[\sum_{i=1}^{m}\|x_i^*\|=1,\qquad \left\|\sum_{i=1}^{m}x_i^*\right\|\le\varepsilon.\] Exact variants replace the approximate inclusions and balance when the normal structure permits.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An abstract extremal principle converts local set separation into normalized approximate normal certificates under axioms imposed on a chosen normal construction.

assumptions_latex: \(f:M\to(-\infty,\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\lambda>0\), there exists \(\bar x\in M\) such that \[d(\bar x,x_0)\le\lambda,\qquad f(\bar x)\le f(x_0),\] and \[f(x)>f(\bar x)-\frac{\varepsilon}{\lambda}d(x,\bar x)\qquad\text{for every }x\ne\bar x.\] Equivalently, \(\bar x\) is the unique minimizer of \(x\mapsto f(x)+(\varepsilon/\lambda)d(x,\bar x)\). This perturbed exact minimum is the variational input for approximate normal and subgradient constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every approximate minimizer of a lower semicontinuous function on a complete metric space yields a nearby exact minimizer after a small distance penalty.

children.title: Smooth Variational Principles
children.top_down_role: Smooth perturbation principles supporting generalized differentiation.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space admitting a \(C^1\)-smooth Lipschitz bump function.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\eta>0\), a bounded \(C^1\)-smooth Lipschitz perturbation \(g\) exists with uniformly small value and derivative such that \(f+g\) has a strong minimum.

notation.meaning: norm controlling the bounded perturbation and its derivative

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deville-Godefroy-Zizler smooth variational principle in the first-order smooth Lipschitz-bump regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\eta>0\), there is a bounded \(C^1\)-smooth Lipschitz function \(g:X\to\mathbb R\) satisfying \[\sup_{x\in X}|g(x)|<\eta,\qquad \sup_{x\in X}\|g'(x)\|<\eta,\] such that \(f+g\) attains a strong minimum at some \(\bar x\in X\). Thus, whenever \((f+g)(x_k)\to(f+g)(\bar x)\), one has \(x_k\to\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Banach space with a continuously differentiable Lipschitz bump, every proper lower-semicontinuous bounded-below function can be given a strong minimum by a perturbation uniformly small in both value and derivative.
knowledge_statements.title: DGZ Smooth Variational Principle

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space supporting the relevant smooth variational principle.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and bounded below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Arbitrarily small smooth perturbations can make \(f\) attain a strong minimum.

The available differentiability class of \(g\) is determined by the smooth bump-function structure of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a suitably smooth Banach space, a lower semicontinuous bounded-below function can be made strongly minimizing by an arbitrarily small smooth perturbation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential and epsilon-enlargement representations for proper locally lower-semicontinuous functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space and let \(\mathcal A(\bar x)\) denote the proper functions \(\varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) that are lower semicontinuous around \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}\varphi\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(X\) is Asplund; (b) for every \(\bar x\in X\) and \(\varphi\in\mathcal A(\bar x)\), \[\partial\varphi(\bar x)=\mathop{\operatorname{Limsup}}_{x\overset{\varphi}{\to}\bar x}\widehat\partial\varphi(x);\] (c) for every such \(\bar x,\varphi\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[\partial_\varepsilon\varphi(\bar x)=\partial\varphi(\bar x)+\varepsilon\mathbb B^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Banach space is Asplund exactly when every proper function that is locally lower semicontinuous admits both the sequential Fréchet-to-limiting subdifferential representation and the stated epsilon-subdifferential enlargement formula.
assumptions_latex: \varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\text{ is proper and lower semicontinuous around }\bar x.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space and \(K\subset X\) is a closed convex cone.
\(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is Fréchet differentiable at a local minimizer \(\bar x\) over \(C:=\bar x+K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The functional \(-\nabla f(\bar x)\) belongs to \(K^\circ\), equivalently \(\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge 0\) for every \(d\in K\).

notation.meaning: Fréchet derivative represented as a dual functional

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the negative polar cone by \[K^\circ:=\{x^*\in X^*:\langle x^*,d\rangle\le 0\ \text{for every }d\in K\}.\] Local minimality of \(f\) on \(C\) yields the verifiable dual certificate \[-\nabla f(\bar x)\in K^\circ.\] Equivalently, \(\langle\nabla f(\bar x),d\rangle\ge 0\) for every feasible direction \(d\in K\). Conversely, this polar inclusion certifies first-order stationarity, though not local minimality without additional convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A polar-cone certificate represents first-order stationarity as nonnegative directional derivative along every feasible cone direction.

A constraint qualification excludes abnormal multipliers at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the constraints \(g_i(x)\le 0\), indexed by \(i=1,\ldots,p\), and \(h_j(x)=0\), indexed by \(j=1,\ldots,q\), there exist multipliers \(\lambda_i\ge 0\) and \(\mu_j\in\mathbb R\) such that \[0=
abla f( ar x)+\sum_{i=1}^p\lambda_i
abla g_i( ar x)+\sum_{j=1}^q\mu_j
abla h_j( ar x),\qquad \lambda_i g_i( ar x)=0.\] The summed multiplier term is a normal generated by the active constraint geometry; together with nontriviality, the displayed relations form a directly checkable stationarity certificate.

assumptions_latex: A Fritz John-type certificate uses an objective multiplier \(\lambda_0\ge 0\) and constraint multipliers \(\lambda\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiplier certificate \((\lambda_0,\lambda)\) is trivial if \((\lambda_0,\lambda)=0\), and it is abnormal if \(\lambda_0=0\) while \(\lambda\ne 0\). The usual normalization \(\lambda_0+\|\lambda\|=1\) removes trivial scaling but does not exclude abnormality. When every available normalized certificate has \(\lambda_0=0\), the objective contributes nothing to the balance relation, so the certificate records only degeneracy of the constraint geometry. A constraint qualification is therefore needed to force \(\lambda_0>0\) and permit normalization to \(\lambda_0=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalization removes the zero certificate, while a constraint qualification is needed to rule out objective-free abnormal multipliers.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-codimension consequences of sequential normal compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and, for convex sets with nonempty relative interior, sufficient finite-codimension conditions for sequential normal compactness in a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space and \(\Omega\subset X\). If \(\Omega\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\in\Omega\), then for every neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \[\operatorname{codim}\overline{\operatorname{aff}}(\Omega\cap U)<\infty.\] In particular, a singleton in \(X\) is sequentially normally compact if and only if \(X\) is finite-dimensional. Moreover, if \(\Omega\) is convex and \(\operatorname{ri}\Omega\neq\varnothing\), then \(\Omega\) is sequentially normally compact at every \(x\in\Omega\) if and only if \(\operatorname{codim}\overline{\operatorname{aff}}\Omega<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SNC at a point forces every neighborhood localization of the set to have a closed affine hull of finite codimension. A singleton is SNC exactly in finite-dimensional spaces. For a convex set with nonempty relative interior, SNC at every point is equivalent to finite codimension of its closed affine hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega\text{ SNC at }\bar x\Rightarrow(\forall U\ni\bar x)\;\operatorname{codim}\overline{\operatorname{aff}}(\Omega\cap U)<\infty;\quad \{x\}\text{ SNC}\Longleftrightarrow\dim X<\infty;\quad [\Omega\text{ convex},\operatorname{ri}\Omega\neq\varnothing]\Rightarrow[\Omega\text{ SNC at every point}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{codim}\overline{\operatorname{aff}}\Omega<\infty].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential normal compactness of a set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise SNC defined through weak-star-null sequences of approximate Fréchet normals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(\Omega\subset X\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\in\Omega\) if, for every sequence \((\varepsilon_k,x_k,x_k^*)\in[0,\infty)\times\Omega\times X^*\) satisfying
\[
\varepsilon_k\downarrow0,\qquad x_k\to\bar x,\qquad x_k^*\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}(x_k;\Omega),\qquad x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}0,
\]
one has \(\|x_k^*\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is sequentially normally compact at a point if every weak-star-null sequence of approximate Fréchet normals at nearby points, with errors decreasing to zero, also converges to zero in norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\varepsilon_k\downarrow0,\ x_k\to\bar x,\ x_k^*\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}(x_k;\Omega),\ x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}0\bigr]\Longrightarrow\|x_k^*\|\to0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential normal compactness and partial sequential normal compactness of multifunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential compactness conditions for approximate coderivative normals to a multifunction graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The mapping \(F\) is SNC at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if every sequence satisfying
\[
\varepsilon_k\downarrow0,\quad (x_k,y_k)\to(\bar x,\bar y),\quad x_k^*\in\widehat D_{\varepsilon_k}^*F(x_k,y_k)(y_k^*),\quad (x_k^*,y_k^*)\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}(0,0)
\]
also satisfies \(\|(x_k^*,y_k^*)\|\to0\). It is PSNC there if the first three conditions together with \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}0\) and \(\|y_k^*\|\to0\) imply \(\|x_k^*\|\to0\). SNC of \(F\) agrees with SNC of \(\operatorname{gph}F\); SNC implies PSNC; PSNC holds whenever \(\dim X<\infty\); and SNC and PSNC coincide whenever \(\dim Y<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SNC requires weak-star convergence of both components of approximate coderivative normals to force their joint norm convergence. PSNC requires this only for the input-dual component when the output-dual component already converges in norm. SNC implies PSNC; PSNC is automatic for finite-dimensional input spaces, and the notions coincide for finite-dimensional output spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{SNC}:\ (x_k^*,y_k^*)\overset{w^*}{\to}(0,0)\Rightarrow\|(x_k^*,y_k^*)\|\to0;\qquad \mathrm{PSNC}:\ x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}0,\ \|y_k^*\|\to0\Rightarrow\|x_k^*\|\to0.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A product-space example separating one-coordinate control from full SNC.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega:=X\times S\) and choose \(u_n:=(0,e_n/n)\to(0,0)\). Since \(e_n/n\) is isolated in \(S\), one has \((0,e_n)\in\widehat N(u_n;\Omega)\). Moreover, \((0,e_n)\) converges weakly to \((0,0)\), its \(X\)-coordinate has norm zero, but \(\|(0,e_n)\|=1\) for every \(n\). Thus every compactness test controlling only the first dual coordinate is satisfied by this sequence, while the full SNC implication fails.

knowledge_statements.title: SNC for Intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-set intersection rule in an Asplund space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated normal qualification, sequential normal compactness of one member is inherited by the intersection: \[\Omega_1\text{ is SNC at }\bar x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\text{ is SNC at }\bar x.\] Explicitly, for every sequence \(x_k\to_{\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2}\bar x\) and \(x_k^*\in\widehat N(x_k;\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2)\) such that \(x_k^*\overset{w^*}{\longrightarrow}0\), one has \(\|x_k^*\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally closed intersection inherits SNC from one constituent when limiting normals from the two sets cannot cancel nontrivially.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space and \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\) are locally closed near \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intersection \(\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\) is SNC at \(\bar x\).

Then \(\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\) is SNC at \(\bar x\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: SNC preservation for a finite intersection of nonsmooth inequality and equality constraint sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For i=1,\ldots,m+r, let \varphi_i:X\to\overline{\mathbb R} satisfy \varphi_i(\bar x)=0. For i\le m, assume \varphi_i is lower semicontinuous around \bar x and SNEC at \bar x; for i>m, assume \varphi_i is continuous around \bar x and SNC at \bar x. Assume 0\notin\partial\varphi_i(\bar x) for i\le m and 0\notin\partial\varphi_i(\bar x)\cup\partial(-\varphi_i)(\bar x) for i>m. Suppose \sum_{i=1}^{m+r}x_i^*=0 implies x_i^*=0 for all i whenever x_i^*\in\mathbb R_+\partial\varphi_i(\bar x)\cup\partial^\infty\varphi_i(\bar x) for i\le m and x_i^*\in\mathbb R_+[\partial\varphi_i(\bar x)\cup\partial(-\varphi_i)(\bar x)]\cup\partial^\infty\varphi_i(\bar x)\cup\partial^\infty(-\varphi_i)(\bar x) for i>m. Define \Omega_i=\{x\mid\varphi_i(x)\le0\} for i\le m and \Omega_i=\{x\mid\varphi_i(x)=0\} for i>m. Then \bigcap_{i=1}^{m+r}\Omega_i is SNC at \bar x.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite intersection of SNEC inequality sets and SNC equality sets is SNC when each constraint satisfies its nonstationarity condition and the specified conic limiting- and singular-subgradient selections admit no nontrivial zero sum.

i>m\Rightarrow \varphi_i\text{ is continuous around }\bar x\text{ and SNC at }\bar x
\sum_{i=1}^{m+r}x_i^*=0\Rightarrow x_i^*=0\ \forall i\text{ for the stated conic limiting- and singular-subgradient selections}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigcap_{i=1}^{m+r}\Omega_i\text{ is SNC at }\bar x

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\times Y\) be locally closed near \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: SNC of Functional Level and Zero Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Functional inverse-image criteria for SNC of a zero sublevel set and a zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \varphi:X\to\overline{\mathbb R} be proper with \varphi(\bar x)=0. (i) If \varphi is lower semicontinuous around \bar x and SNEC at \bar x, then \Omega=\{x\in X\mid\varphi(x)\le 0\} is SNC at \bar x provided that 0\notin\partial\varphi(\bar x). (ii) If \varphi is continuous around \bar x and SNC at \bar x, then \Omega=\{x\in X\mid\varphi(x)=0\} is SNC at \bar x provided that 0\notin\partial\varphi(\bar x)\cup\partial(-\varphi)(\bar x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-semicontinuous SNEC function has an SNC zero sublevel set under the stated nonstationarity condition. A continuous SNC function has an SNC zero set when neither it nor its negative has zero as a limiting subgradient.
assumptions_latex: \text{For (i): }\varphi\text{ is l.s.c. around }\bar x,\ \varphi\text{ is SNEC at }\bar x,\ 0\notin\partial\varphi(\bar x)
\text{For (ii): }\varphi\text{ is continuous around }\bar x,\ \varphi\text{ is SNC at }\bar x,\ 0\notin\partial\varphi(\bar x)\cup\partial(-\varphi)(\bar x)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x\mid\varphi(x)\le0\}\text{ is SNC at }\bar x\text{ under (i), and }\{x\mid\varphi(x)=0\}\text{ is SNC at }\bar x\text{ under (ii)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed Qualification Condition for Two Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential qualification for two subsets of a product of Banach spaces, together with its normal-qualification sufficient condition and limiting-qualification failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\times Y\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\). The pair satisfies the mixed qualification condition at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with respect to \(Y\) if, for every \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), \((x_{ik},y_{ik})\xrightarrow{\Omega_i}(\bar x,\bar y)\), \((x_{ik}^*,y_{ik}^*)\xrightarrow{w^*}(x_i^*,y_i^*)\), and \((x_{ik}^*,y_{ik}^*)\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}((x_{ik},y_{ik});\Omega_i)\), \(i=1,2\), the conditions \(x_{1k}^*+x_{2k}^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0\) and \(\|y_{1k}^*+y_{2k}^*\|\to0\) imply \((x_1^*,y_1^*)=(x_2^*,y_2^*)=(0,0)\). If \(X\) and \(Y\) are Asplund and both sets are locally closed near the reference point, one may take \(\varepsilon_k=0\). The normal qualification \(N((\bar x,\bar y);\Omega_1)\cap[-N((\bar x,\bar y);\Omega_2)]=\{(0,0)\}\) implies the mixed condition. The limiting qualification condition is weaker but does not suffice for SNC calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The mixed qualification condition rules out nonzero limiting normals whose X-components cancel weak-star while their Y-components cancel in norm. Normal qualification implies it; the weaker limiting qualification alone is insufficient for SNC calculus.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal and limiting qualification conditions for two sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise and sequential qualification conditions used in limiting-normal intersection calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\), where \(X\) is Banach, and let \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\). The normal qualification condition is \(N(\bar x;\Omega_1)\cap[-N(\bar x;\Omega_2)]=\{0\}\). The limiting qualification condition requires that for every \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), \(x_{ik}\xrightarrow{\Omega_i}\bar x\), and \(x_{ik}^*\overset{w^*}{\to}x_i^*\) with \(x_{ik}^*\in\widehat N_{\varepsilon_k}(x_{ik};\Omega_i)\), the implication \(\|x_{1k}^*+x_{2k}^*\|\to0\Rightarrow x_1^*=x_2^*=0\) holds. If \(X\) is Asplund and both sets are closed around \(\bar x\), one may equivalently take \(\varepsilon_k=0\). For locally closed sets in an Asplund space, the normal qualification condition is equivalent to the corresponding implication when \(x_{1k}^*+x_{2k}^*\overset{w^*}{\to}0\). The two qualification conditions are equivalent in finite dimensions, whereas the limiting condition may be weaker in infinite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal qualification excludes nonzero opposing limiting normals at the reference point. Limiting qualification excludes nonzero weak-star limits of approximate normals whose sums converge to zero in norm. They coincide in finite dimensions but can differ in infinite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{NQC}:\ N(\bar x;\Omega_1)\cap[-N(\bar x;\Omega_2)]=\{0\};\quad \mathrm{LQC}:\ \|x_{1k}^*+x_{2k}^*\|\to0\Rightarrow x_1^*=x_2^*=0\) under the stated sequential hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by omitting target-set SNC, even for an identity map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_n:=e_n/n\). The sequence satisfies \(x_n\to0\), \(e_n\in\widehat N(x_n;S)\), \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\), and \(\|e_n\|=1\) for every \(n\). Hence \(S\) is not SNC at \(0\). For the identity mapping \(f:H\to H\), one has \(f^{-1}(S)=S\), so linearity, smoothness, and invertibility of \(f\) do not replace the target-set SNC hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed non-SNC target remains non-SNC under the identity inverse image, so mapping regularity cannot replace target-set SNC.
assumptions_latex: \(H=\ell^2\), \(S:=\{0\}\cup\{e_n/n:n\in\mathbb N\}\), and \(f:H\to H\) is the identity mapping.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f\) is linear and invertible, \(f^{-1}(S)=S\) is not SNC at \(0\).

children.title: Algebraic SNC Preservation Calculus
children.top_down_role: Compactness preservation for additive and product mapping operations.

children.title: SNC under Set Addition
children.top_down_role: Compactness preservation for Minkowski-type additive constructions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Translation Invariance of Sequential Normal Compactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The fixed-vector specialization of Minkowski addition in a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\subset X\), \(b\in X\), and \(\bar a\in A\). Translation gives \[\widehat N(a+b;A+b)=\widehat N(a;A)\qquad(a\in A),\] and therefore \[A+b\text{ is SNC at }\bar a+b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A\text{ is SNC at }\bar a.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Translation by a fixed vector preserves and reflects sequential normal compactness.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Banach space, \(A\subset X\), \(b\in X\), and \(\bar a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A+b\) is SNC at \(\bar a+b\) if and only if \(A\) is SNC at \(\bar a\).
knowledge_statements.title: Translation Invariance of Sequential Normal Compactness

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and \(A,B\subset X\) are nonempty.
\(A+B:=\{a+b:a\in A,\ b\in B\}\) is locally closed near \(\bar x\in A+B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Minkowski sum \(A+B\) is SNC at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional addition regime; no infinite-dimensional preservation claim is made.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every sequence \(x_k\to_{A+B}\bar x\) and every choice \(x_k^*\in\widehat N(x_k;A+B)\), weak-star convergence \(x_k^*\to0\) implies norm convergence \(\|x_k^*\|\to0\). Therefore \(A+B\) is SNC at \(\bar x\). The conclusion follows from finite dimensionality and local closedness of the resulting sum; it does not assert that set addition preserves SNC in arbitrary infinite-dimensional spaces or without local closedness of \(A+B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally closed Minkowski sum is automatically SNC in finite dimensions, independently of compactness properties of its summands.
knowledge_statements.title: SNC under Set Addition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conclusion is mathematically standard from finite-dimensional automatic compactness, but no citation is supplied. It describes only an automatic finite-dimensional case, not a substantive set-addition preservation theorem, so exact source and scope support are required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternative sufficient conditions based on inner semicompactness or inner semicontinuity of the decomposition mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\) be closed, let \(\bar x\in\Omega_1+\Omega_2\), and define \(S(x):=\{(x_1,x_2)\in X\times X:x_1+x_2=x,\ x_1\in\Omega_1,\ x_2\in\Omega_2\}\). Then \(\Omega_1+\Omega_2\) is SNC at \(\bar x\) if either: (a) \(S\) is inner semicompact at \(\bar x\), and for every \((x_1,x_2)\in S(\bar x)\), at least one of \(\Omega_1\) at \(x_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) at \(x_2\) is SNC; or (b) for some \((\bar x_1,\bar x_2)\in S(\bar x)\), \(S\) is inner semicontinuous at \((\bar x_1,\bar x_2,\bar x)\), and at least one of \(\Omega_1\) at \(\bar x_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) at \(\bar x_2\) is SNC.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sum of two closed sets is SNC if its decomposition mapping is inner semicompact and every decomposition has an SNC summand, or if the mapping is inner semicontinuous at one decomposition having an SNC summand.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega_1+\Omega_2\text{ is SNC at }\bar x
