knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contingent sum rule separating synchronized inner inclusion from exact tangent decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H(x):=\sum_{i=1}^mF_i(x)\) and \(\bar y=\sum_i\bar y_i\), with \(\bar y_i\in F_i(\bar x)\). If component tangent arcs for a common direction \(u\) can be synchronized, then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^mDF_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(u)\subset DH(\bar x,\bar y)(u).
\]
If, in addition, every tangent to \(\operatorname{gph}H\) lifts to a compatible value decomposition and all such component tangents are synchronizable, then
\[
DH(\bar x,\bar y)(u)=\bigcup_{\substack{\bar y_i\in F_i(\bar x)\\\sum_i\bar y_i=\bar y}}\sum_{i=1}^mDF_i(\bar x,\bar y_i)(u).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronized component tangents add to a sum tangent; equality requires every sum tangent to lift to a compatible component decomposition.
assumptions_latex: The inner inclusion uses synchronized component tangent arcs.
The equality additionally uses exhaustive tangent lifting over compatible reference-value decompositions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inner inclusion holds under synchronization and becomes equality under two-sided tangent decomposition.
knowledge_statements.title: Graphical-Derivative Sum Rule

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact contingent chain representation under explicit two-sided tangent lifting through intermediate points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(H:=G\circ F\) and \(K(x,z):=F(x)\cap G^{-1}(z)\). Suppose every tangent to \(\operatorname{gph}H\) at \((\bar x,\bar z)\) lifts through some \(\bar y\in K(\bar x,\bar z)\), and every compatible pair \((u,v)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}F}(\bar x,\bar y)\), \((v,w)\in T_{\operatorname{gph}G}(\bar y,\bar z)\) is realizable by synchronized graph arcs of the composition. Then
\[
DH(\bar x,\bar z)(u)=\bigcup_{\bar y\in K(\bar x,\bar z)}\ \bigcup_{v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)}DG(\bar y,\bar z)(v).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When composition tangents lift and component tangent arcs can be synchronized, graphical derivatives propagate directions successively through the two mappings.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \(G:Y\rightrightarrows Z\) act between finite-dimensional spaces.
The stated two-sided tangent-lifting and synchronization property holds at \((\bar x,\bar z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(DH(\bar x,\bar z)(u)=\bigcup_{\bar y\in K(\bar x,\bar z)}\bigcup_{v\in DF(\bar x,\bar y)(u)}DG(\bar y,\bar z)(v)\).

assumptions_latex: \(f_1,f_2:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), with \(f_1(\bar x)\) and \(f_2(\bar x)\) finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\cap(-\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x))=\{0\}\), then \(\partial(f_1+f_2)(\bar x)\subset\partial f_1(\bar x)+\partial f_2(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-function finite-dimensional qualification excluding cancellation of horizontal epigraph normals.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The singular-subgradient qualification for addition is
\[
\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.
\]
Equivalently, if \(x_1^*\in\partial^\infty f_1(\bar x)\), \(x_2^*\in\partial^\infty f_2(\bar x)\), and \(x_1^*+x_2^*=0\), then \(x_1^*=x_2^*=0\). Under this qualification,
\[
\partial(f_1+f_2)(\bar x)
\subset
\partial f_1(\bar x)+\partial f_2(\bar x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposing nonzero singular subgradients are excluded; for lower-semicontinuous functions in finite dimensions, this yields the limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular-Subgradient Qualifications

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.1 Calculus Rules for Basic and Singular Subgradients p. 296
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family extension of the limiting-subdifferential sum qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) and finite at \(\bar x\), with \(X\) finite-dimensional. If \[x_i^*\in\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1^*=\cdots=x_m^*=0,\] then \[\partial\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite sum, exclusion of every nontrivial balanced tuple of singular subgradients yields the limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion.
assumptions_latex: Each \(f_i\) is lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\) and finite at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i)(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^m\partial f_i(\bar x).\)
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Singular Qualification

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Automatic finite-sum singular qualification when all but at most one summand are locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\), then \[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)=\{0\}.\] Consequently, the finite-sum singular no-balancing qualification holds automatically whenever all but at most one summand are locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local Lipschitzness annihilates the singular subdifferential, so a finite sum is automatically singularly qualified when at most one summand is non-Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: All but at most one of \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f_i(\bar x)=\{0\}\) for every locally Lipschitz summand, and the finite-sum singular qualification holds automatically.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Lipschitz Sufficient Regime

children.title: Normal-Cone Transversality
children.top_down_role: Geometric opposition conditions for intersections and inverse images.

assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\) are locally closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Transversality yields the limiting-normal intersection inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional normal-cone opposition condition for intersections; inverse-image qualifications follow by applying it to lifted graph sets.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sets \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) are normally transversal at \(\bar x\) when
\[
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.
\]
Under this condition, the limiting normal cone to their intersection satisfies
\[
N_{\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2}(\bar x)
\subset
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)+N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x).
\]
The same condition applied to graph and constraint sets supplies the geometric qualification for inverse-image and generalized-equation calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two sets are transversal when their limiting normals cannot oppose nontrivially; then intersection normals decompose into normals to the individual sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Cone Transversality

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.1 Calculus of Normal Cones p. 262
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family extension of the two-set normal-cone qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\) be locally closed subsets of a finite-dimensional normed space and let \(\bar x\in\bigcap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i\). If \[x_i^*\in N_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\ (i=1,\ldots,m),\qquad \sum_{i=1}^m x_i^*=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x_1^*=\cdots=x_m^*=0,\] then \[N_{\cap_{i=1}^m\Omega_i}(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_{i=1}^mN_{\Omega_i}(\bar x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite set family is normally transversal when no nontrivial selection of limiting normals balances to zero; then intersection normals decompose into component normals.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_1,\ldots,\Omega_m\) are locally closed in a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\cap_i\Omega_i}(\bar x)\subseteq\sum_iN_{\Omega_i}(\bar x)\) under the no-balancing condition.

notation.meaning: limiting normal cone to the ith set

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Family Normal Transversality

children.top_down_role: Metric regularity and normal-compactness regimes supporting calculus.

children.title: Metric-Regularity Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Metric stability regimes supporting generalized differential calculus.

assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\) in finite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed coderivative-kernel condition is equivalent to metric regularity around \((\bar x,\bar y)\).

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Mordukhovich coderivative criterion for metric regularity.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.3 Metric Regularity and Covering p. 56
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) is metrically regular around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) precisely when there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\kappa>0\) such that
\[
d(x,F^{-1}(y))\leq\kappa d(y,F(x))
\quad\text{for all }(x,y)\in U\times V,
\]
and this is equivalent to the coderivative qualification
\[
0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*)
\Longrightarrow y^*=0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Metric regularity is equivalent, in finite dimensions, to the absence of nonzero dual vectors mapped to zero by the coderivative.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Regularity Qualifications

children.title: Normal-Compactness Qualifications
children.top_down_role: Sequential compactness regimes controlling limiting normal behavior.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an Asplund space and \(\Omega\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\).
Normals in the sequential test are Fréchet normals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed implication defines sequential normal compactness at \(\bar x\).

notation.meaning: weak-star convergence in the dual space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential normal compactness for sets in Asplund spaces; it is automatic in finite dimensions.

source_refs.locator: 1.1.4 Sequential Normal Compactness of Sets p. 27
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(\Omega\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\in\Omega\) if every pair of sequences satisfying
\[
x_k\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x,
\qquad x_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(x_k),
\qquad x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0
\]
also satisfies
\[
\|x_k^*\|\to0.
\]
Thus weak-star disappearance of nearby Fréchet normals cannot occur while their norms remain bounded away from zero. In finite-dimensional spaces, weak-star and norm convergence coincide, so this property holds automatically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential normal compactness requires weak-star vanishing nearby Fréchet normals to vanish in norm; finite-dimensional sets satisfy it automatically.
knowledge_statements.title: Normal-Compactness Qualifications

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.4 Sequential Normal Compactness of Sets p. 27
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Metric–Compactness Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Interactions between metric stability and normal compactness assumptions.

assumptions_latex: \(X\) is Asplund, and \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\) are locally closed at \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\).
At least one set is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\).
The limiting-normal transversality condition holds at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The intersection is sequentially normally compact and obeys the limiting-normal sum inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of normal transversality and sequential compactness in Asplund-space intersection calculus.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose
\[
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\},
\]
and at least one of \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\). Then \(\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\), and
\[
N_{\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2}(\bar x)
\subset
N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)+N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x).
\]
Transversality removes abnormal cancellation, while normal compactness prevents nonvanishing multiplier mass from disappearing only in the weak-star topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normal transversality and sequential normal compactness together preserve compactness and yield the limiting-normal intersection rule.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric–Compactness Compatibility

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.1 Sequential Normal Compactness of Set Intersections and Inverse Images p. 341
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transversality as Metric Regularity of the Intersection Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional metric interpretation of the normal qualification used in compactness-supported intersection calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega_1,\Omega_2\subset X\) be locally closed near \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\), where \(X\) is finite-dimensional, and define \[\Phi(x):=(\Omega_1-x)\times(\Omega_2-x).\] Then \(\Phi\) is metrically regular around \((\bar x,(0,0))\) if and only if \[N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap\bigl(-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)\bigr)=\{0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two locally closed finite-dimensional sets, normal transversality is equivalent to metric regularity of the lifted mapping encoding their intersection.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega_1\) and \(\Omega_2\) are locally closed near \(\bar x\in\Omega_1\cap\Omega_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi\text{ is metrically regular around }(\bar x,(0,0))\iff N_{\Omega_1}(\bar x)\cap[-N_{\Omega_2}(\bar x)]=\{0\}.\)

notation.meaning: lifted multifunction encoding simultaneous membership in both sets

knowledge_statements.title: Transversality as Metric Regularity of the Intersection Mapping

children.title: Qualification Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Calculus losses caused by failure of metric or compactness support.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper and lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\cap[-\partial^\infty g(\bar x)]\ne\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Mordukhovich singular subdifferential of f at x

review_flags: Failure of the qualification does not itself assert failure of every calculus conclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the standard singular-subgradient qualification for a limiting sum rule.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The singular-subgradient qualification for the limiting sum rule fails at \(\bar x\) precisely when
\[\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\cap[-\partial^\infty g(\bar x)]\ne\{0\}.\]
Equivalently, there is a nonzero \(v\) with \(v\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x)\) and \(-v\in\partial^\infty g(\bar x)\). In this regime the usual qualification-based derivation of \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subset\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\) is unavailable; the condition alone does not imply that the inclusion is false.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Qualification fails when the summands possess nonzero opposite singular subgradients. The standard sum-rule theorem then becomes inapplicable, although its conclusion may still hold accidentally.
knowledge_statements.title: Qualification Failure Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact sequential failure boundary for the compactness component of the parent qualification architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A locally closed set \(\Omega\subset X\) fails to be sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\in\Omega\) exactly when there exist sequences \[x_k\xrightarrow{\Omega}\bar x,\qquad x_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(x_k),\qquad x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0,\] for which \(\|x_k^*\|\not\to0\). After passage to a subsequence and positive normalization, the witness can be chosen with \(\|x_k^*\|=1\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SNC fails precisely when nearby Fréchet normals vanish weak-star without vanishing in norm; unit-norm witnesses can be used.
assumptions_latex: \(\Omega\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Omega\text{ is not SNC at }\bar x\iff\exists x_k\to_\Omega\bar x,\ x_k^*\in\widehat N_\Omega(x_k),\ x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0,\ \|x_k^*\|\not\to0.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Normal-Compactness Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional failure boundary for the metric component of the parent qualification architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) have locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\) in finite-dimensional spaces. The metric-regularity qualification fails exactly when \[\ker D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\ne\{0\},\] equivalently, when some \(y^*\ne0\) satisfies \[0\in D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)(y^*).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the metric qualification fails exactly when a nonzero output covector is mapped to zero by the coderivative.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) has locally closed graph near \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is not metrically regular around }(\bar x,\bar y)\iff\ker D^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\ne\{0\}.\)

notation.meaning: output covectors whose coderivative image contains zero

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Regularity Qualification Failure

children.title: One-Sided Calculus Inclusions
children.top_down_role: Calculus outcomes limited to a single containment direction.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper and lower semicontinuous near \(\bar x\), and \(f\) is locally Lipschitz there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of subsets of the dual space

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional limiting-subdifferential sum rule with a Lipschitz summand.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the Mordukhovich limiting subdifferential, local Lipschitz continuity of one summand removes its nonzero singular subgradients and yields the one-sided estimate
\[\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\subseteq\partial f(\bar x)+\partial g(\bar x).\]
This statement is only an upper calculus inclusion: it does not assert that every vector formed by adding a member of \(\partial f(\bar x)\) to a member of \(\partial g(\bar x)\) belongs to \(\partial(f+g)(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With one summand locally Lipschitz, every limiting subgradient of the sum decomposes into subgradients of the summands; the reverse inclusion need not hold.
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Calculus Inclusions

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Equality Recovery Regimes
children.top_down_role: Additional structure restoring equality from one-sided estimates.

assumptions_latex: \(f,g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) are proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex exact sum rule under relative-interior qualification.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If the relative interiors of the effective domains meet, then for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\cap\operatorname{dom}g\) the convex subdifferential satisfies the exact sum rule
\[\partial(f+g)(x)=\partial f(x)+\partial g(x).\]
Thus both the upper calculus inclusion and its reverse hold. In finite dimensions the convex and Mordukhovich limiting subdifferentials coincide for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions, so the equality also supplies an equality-recovery regime for limiting calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For proper closed convex functions whose domain relative interiors intersect, the subdifferential of their sum equals the Minkowski sum of their subdifferentials.
knowledge_statements.title: Equality Recovery Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

children.title: Sharpness Loss
children.top_down_role: Regimes where valid calculus estimates substantially overapproximate the target object.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial(f+g)(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq[-2,2]=\partial f(0)+\partial g(0)\).
review_flags: The cited section supports limiting-subdifferential calculus; the displayed example requires direct source confirmation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete strictness example for the limiting-subdifferential sum inclusion.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At the origin, \(f+g\equiv0\), while
\[\partial f(0)=[-1,1],\qquad \partial g(0)=\{-1,1\}.\]
Consequently,
\[\partial(f+g)(0)=\{0\}\subsetneq[-2,2]=\partial f(0)+\partial g(0).\]
Both functions are locally Lipschitz, so the applicable one-sided sum estimate can be strictly larger than the true limiting subdifferential even when its qualification is satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The functions absolute value and minus absolute value sum to zero, but the sum of their limiting subdifferentials strictly overestimates the exact subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharpness Loss

children.title: Vacuous Estimate Regimes
children.top_down_role: Failures yielding formally valid but structurally uninformative inclusions.

assumptions_latex: A calculus rule produces an upper estimate \(\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq E(\bar x)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The estimate is vacuous at \(\bar x\) exactly when \(E(\bar x)=\mathbb{R}^n\).
review_flags: Terminological definition synthesized from the information content of a calculus inclusion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vacuity is defined relative to an ambient finite-dimensional dual space.

source_refs.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_refs.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An upper calculus estimate \(\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq E(\bar x)\) is vacuous at \(\bar x\) when
\[E(\bar x)=\mathbb{R}^n.\]
The displayed inclusion then reduces to the ambient fact \(\partial F(\bar x)\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and excludes no candidate subgradient. More generally, vacuity relative to a prescribed admissible set \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) means \(E(\bar x)\supseteq A\), so the estimate supplies no restriction beyond prior admissibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A calculus upper bound is vacuous when it equals the entire ambient dual space, and therefore rules out no possible subgradient.
knowledge_statements.title: Vacuous Estimate Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: 1.3.4 Subdifferential Calculus in Banach Spaces p. 112
source_witnesses.source_title: Variational Analysis and Generalized Differentiation I

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute vacuity for a one-sided lower estimate in a finite-dimensional dual space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A lower calculus estimate \(L(\bar x)\subseteq\partial F(\bar x)\) is vacuous at \(\bar x\) when \[L(\bar x)=\varnothing.\] It then certifies no subgradient of \(F\) at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower subdifferential estimate is vacuous when it is empty and therefore certifies no subgradient.
assumptions_latex: A calculus rule produces a lower estimate \(L(\bar x)\subseteq\partial F(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L(\bar x)=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.title: Vacuous Lower Calculus Estimates

children.title: Second Directional Derivatives
children.top_down_role: Directional second-order growth constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), \(\bar x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and the finite directional derivative \(f'(\bar x;h)\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f''(\bar x;h)=\displaystyle\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)-t f'(\bar x;h)}{\tfrac12t^2}\), when this limit exists finitely.

notation.meaning: first directional derivative at x along h
second directional derivative at x along h

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ray-based second directional derivative normalized by one-half squared step length.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The second directional derivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) in direction \(h\) is the finite limit
\[f''(\bar x;h):=\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{f(\bar x+th)-f(\bar x)-t f'(\bar x;h)}{\tfrac12t^2},\]
provided this one-sided limit exists. With this normalization, if \(f\) is twice Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar x\), then \(f''(\bar x;h)=\langle h,\nabla^2f(\bar x)h\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second directional derivative is the quadratic-order remainder along a fixed ray after subtracting the first directional term.
knowledge_statements.title: Second Directional Derivatives

source_witnesses.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f''(\bar x;h)\ge0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Raywise second-order necessary condition after the first-order term vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\bar x\) is a local minimizer, \(f'(\bar x;h)=0\), and the finite second directional derivative exists, then \[f''(\bar x;h)\ge0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a local minimizer, every direction with zero first-order growth has nonnegative existing second directional curvature.
knowledge_statements.title: Second Directional Necessary Condition

assumptions_latex: The finite first and second one-sided directional derivatives exist in direction \(h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f''(\bar x;\lambda h)=\lambda^2f''(\bar x;h).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling property of the fixed-ray second directional derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the relevant second directional derivatives exist, then for every \(\lambda>0\), \[f''(\bar x;\lambda h)=\lambda^2f''(\bar x;h).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second directional derivative is positively homogeneous of degree two in its direction.
knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Positive Homogeneity

children.title: Second Subderivatives
children.top_down_role: Epigraphical second-order growth models.

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, \(f(\bar x)\) is finite, and \(\bar v\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w)=\displaystyle\liminf_{t\downarrow0,\,w'\to w}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w'\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2}\).

notation.meaning: lower limit over positive t and perturbed directions

review_flags: The supplied locator concerns second-order directional derivatives; exact terminology should be checked.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rockafellar-type lower second epi-derivative relative to a reference subgradient.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(w\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the second subderivative of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\bar v\) is
\[d^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\w'\to w}}\frac{f(\bar x+t w')-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w'\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2}.\]
It is an extended-real function of \(w\); the perturbation \(w'\to w\) makes it a lower epigraphical second-order growth construction rather than a fixed-ray limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second subderivative is the lower quadratic growth after subtracting a reference linear form, allowing nearby directions as the step tends to zero.
knowledge_statements.title: Second Subderivatives

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-subderivative tests for local optimality and second-order growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary nonnegativity, finite-dimensional strict-positivity characterization, and reduction of strict testing to critical directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let x_0 be feasible for (P). If x_0 is a local minimizer, then d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)\ge0 for every h\in X. If X is finite dimensional, the second-order growth condition at x_0 holds if and only if d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)>0 for every h\in X\setminus\{0\}. Furthermore, f_-^{\downarrow}(x_0,h)>0 implies d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)=+\infty. Hence, if f_-^{\downarrow}(x_0,\cdot)\ge0, strict second-order conditions need only be checked on C(x_0)\setminus\{0\}, where C(x_0)=\{h\in X:f_-^{\downarrow}(x_0,h)=0\}; this cone need not be convex when f is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local minimizer has a nonnegative second subderivative in every direction. In finite dimensions, strict positivity in every nonzero direction characterizes second-order growth. Directions of positive first-order growth have infinite second subderivative, so under the first-order condition it suffices to test nonzero critical directions; the critical cone may be nonconvex for a nonconvex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_0\text{ locally optimal}\Rightarrow d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)\ge0\ \forall h;\quad \dim X<\infty\Rightarrow[\text{second-order growth}\Longleftrightarrow d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)>0\ \forall h\ne0];\quad f_-^{\downarrow}(x_0,h)>0\Rightarrow d^2f(x_0\mid0)(h)=+\infty

The basic second-order subdifferential of \(f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) is the coderivative of its limiting-subdifferential mapping:

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar smooth example separating projection of the full response from a zero-parameter-covector restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x,p)=xp\), one has \(S(x,p)=\partial_xf(x,p)=\{p\}\) and \[D^*S((0,0),0)(u)=\{(0,u)\}.\] Hence the decision-coordinate projection is \(\{0\}\) for every \(u\), whereas \(\{w:(w,0)\in D^*S((0,0),0)(u)\}\) is empty whenever \(u\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even for a smooth coupled function, projecting the full coderivative output differs from requiring the parameter component to vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(u\ne0\), \(\operatorname{proj}_X D^*S((0,0),0)(u)=\{0\}\) but \(\{w:(w,0)\in D^*S((0,0),0)(u)\}=\varnothing\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Full Coderivative Response of a Partial Subgradient Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats the coderivative's full product-space output as primary; coordinate projections and zero-coordinate slices are distinct derived constructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S(x,p):=\partial_x f(x,p)\). For \(u\in X\), define the full partial second-order response by \[\mathcal H_x f((\bar x,\bar p),\bar v)(u):=D^*S((\bar x,\bar p),\bar v)(u)\subset X\times P.\] Its decision and parameter responses are the coordinate projections of this set. Requiring an output of the form \((w,0)\) is a separate zero-parameter-covector slice and is not generally equivalent to projecting onto the decision coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The coderivative of the partial subgradient mapping has a full product-space output; coordinate projections must not be confused with imposing a zero value in another coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\times P\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*(\partial_x f)((\bar x,\bar p),\bar v)(u)\subset X\times P\), with projections and zero-coordinate slices constituting distinct derived objects.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The subgradient mapping is proto-differentiable at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) when the difference-quotient mappings \[Q_t(u):=\frac{\partial f(\bar x+tu)-\bar v}{t}\] converge graphically as \(t\downarrow0\). children.title: Twice Epi-Differentiability
children.top_down_role: Stable second-order epigraphical approximation and its mapping consequences.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates existence of an epi-limit from the additional requirement that the limit be proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), set \[\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+tw)-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w\rangle}{\tfrac12t^2}.\] The function is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) when \(\Delta_t^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) epi-converges as \(t\downarrow0\); its epi-limit is \(d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\). It is properly twice epi-differentiable when this epi-limit is additionally a proper extended-real function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twice epi-differentiability requires an epi-limit of normalized second-order quotients; proper twice epi-differentiability additionally requires that limit to be proper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ordinary twice epi-differentiability asserts epi-convergence; proper twice epi-differentiability adds properness of \(d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary and Proper Twice Epi-Differentiability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex correspondence under the one-half squared-step normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper lower semicontinuous convex function, proper twice epi-differentiability of \(f\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) is equivalent to proto-differentiability of \(\partial f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\). In that case, \[D(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)(w)=\partial\!\left(\tfrac12d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\right)(w)\qquad(w\in X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex function, proper twice epi-differentiability is equivalent to proto-differentiability of the subgradient mapping, with the proto-derivative represented by the subdifferential of half the second epi-derivative.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(\partial f)(\bar x,\bar v)=\partial(\tfrac12d_e^2f(\bar x\mid\bar v))\) whenever the equivalent proper twice-epi/proto-differentiability conditions hold.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Proto-Derivative Correspondence

assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, with \(\bar v\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) exactly when \(\Delta_t^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v)\) epi-converges as \(t\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the normalization with denominator one-half times the squared step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(t>0\), define the second-order difference quotient by \[\Delta_t^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v)(w):=\frac{f(\bar x+tw)-f(\bar x)-t\langle\bar v,w\rangle}{\tfrac12 t^{2}}.\] The function \(f\) is twice epi-differentiable at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if these functions epi-converge as \(t\downarrow0\). The resulting proper extended-real function, when it exists, is \[d_e^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v):=\operatorname{e-lim}_{t\downarrow0}\Delta_t^{2}f(\bar x\mid\bar v).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twice epi-differentiability means that normalized second-order difference quotients have a well-defined epigraphical limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Twice Epi-Differentiability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalization and epi-convergence formulation are recognizable standard definitions, but the record has no citation. Moreover, calling the resulting epi-limit proper may require the stronger notion of proper twice epi-differentiability rather than twice epi-differentiability alone. An authoritative definition with an exact locator is required before choosing the correct formulation.

children.title: Second-Order Convex Duality
children.top_down_role: Dual correspondence among second-order convex constructions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex duality under the half-quadratic normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(q_f=d_e^2f(x\mid v)\) and \(q_{f^*}=d_e^2f^*(v\mid x)\), where the second-order difference quotients use denominator \(\tfrac12t^2\). Then
\[
\frac12q_{f^*}=\left(\frac12q_f\right)^{\star},
\]
where \(\star\) on the right denotes Fenchel conjugation. Consequently,
\[
\partial\!\left(\frac12q_{f^*}\right)=\left[\partial\!\left(\frac12q_f\right)\right]^{-1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At conjugate graph points, the half-scaled convex second epi-derivatives are Fenchel conjugates, so their subdifferentials are inverse relations.
assumptions_latex: \(X=\mathbb R^n\) and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
The second epi-derivatives of \(f\) at \((x,v)\) and \(f^*\) at \((v,x)\) exist as proper closed convex functions under the denominator \(\tfrac12t^2\) convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tfrac12d_e^2f^*(v\mid x)=\bigl(\tfrac12d_e^2f(x\mid v)\bigr)^{\star}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(q=d_e^2f(x\mid v)\) and \(q^*=d_e^2f^*(v\mid x)\) through epi-limits of the second-order difference quotients with denominator \(\tfrac12t^2\). Then the primal and conjugate second epi-derivatives satisfy
\[
\frac12 q^*(z)=\sup_{w\in X}\left\{\langle z,w\rangle-\frac12q(w)\right\}
\quad\text{for every }z\in X.
\]
Consequently, \(\partial(\tfrac12q)\) and \(\partial(\tfrac12q^*)\) are inverse relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At conjugate primal-dual points, the half-scaled second epi-derivatives are Fenchel conjugates, and their subdifferential relations are inverses.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete oscillatory failure when second-order directional regularity is absent.

source_refs.locator: 4.2 Second-Order Directional Derivatives p. 162

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Although \(f\) is differentiable at \(0\) with \(f'(0)=0\), its second-order quotient in direction \(1\) is
\[
Q_t=\frac{f(t)-f(0)-t f'(0)}{\tfrac12t^2}=2\sin(1/t).
\]
Thus \(Q_t\) has no limit as \(t\downarrow0\). Removing second-order directional regularity therefore destroys the ordinary second directional derivative at the reference point; identities or chain rules requiring that derivative, twice epi-differentiability, or a compatible second-order limit are not applicable without additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oscillating quadratic perturbation is differentiable at zero but has no second directional derivative there, blocking calculus that requires a stable second-order limit.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if there exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(r\ge0\) such that
\[
f(x')\ge f(x)+\langle v,x'-x\rangle-\frac r2\lVert x'-x\rVert^2
\]
whenever \(\lVert x-\bar x\rVert<\varepsilon\), \(\lvert f(x)-f(\bar x)\rvert<\varepsilon\), \(v\in\partial f(x)\), \(\lVert v-\bar v\rVert<\varepsilon\), and \(\lVert x'-\bar x\rVert<\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity requires nearby subgradients to support the function locally up to one uniform negative quadratic error.
knowledge_statements.title: Prox-Regularity

This localization is the local proximal branch and has Lipschitz modulus at most \((1-\lambda r)^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a sufficiently small proximal parameter, prox-regularity yields a locally single-valued Lipschitz proximal branch.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\), with attentive hypomonotonicity modulus \(r\).
The subgradient mapping and resolvent are localized at the specified graph points.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional subgradient-attentive characterization at a selected graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is prox-regular at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar v\) if and only if an \(f\)-attentive localization \(T\) of \(\partial f\) at \((\bar x,\bar v)\) and \(r\ge0\) exist such that
\[
\langle v_1-v_2,x_1-x_2\rangle\ge-r\|x_1-x_2\|^2
\]
for all \((x_i,v_i)\in\operatorname{gph}T\). Equivalently, \(T+rI\) is monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prox-regularity at a selected subgradient is equivalent to hypomonotonicity of an attentive localization of the subgradient mapping.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.

children.title: Tilt-Stability Interface
children.top_down_role: Second-order generalized derivative diagnostics for stable local minimizers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional localized-argmin definition under linear perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\gamma>0\), define
\[
M_\gamma(v)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\|x-\bar x\|\le\gamma}\{f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\}.
\]
The point \(\bar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer if, for some \(\gamma>0\), \(M_\gamma\) has a single-valued Lipschitz localization near \(v=0\) and \(M_\gamma(0)=\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tilt stability means that the localized minimizer under a small linear tilt is unique and Lipschitz in the tilt.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(\bar x\) is a local minimizer with \(f(\bar x)<+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M_\gamma\) is locally single-valued and Lipschitz at \((0,\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: localized argmin mapping under a linear tilt

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional prox-regular characterization using nearby attentive graph points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The point \(\bar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer if and only if there are \(\eta>0\) and \(c>0\) such that
\[
\langle w,u\rangle\ge c\|u\|^2
\]
for every \(u\in\mathbb R^n\), every \(w\in\partial^2f(x,v)(u)\), and every sufficiently close \(f\)-attentive graph point \((x,v)\in\operatorname{gph}\partial f\) satisfying \(\|(x,v)-(\bar x,0)\|<\eta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a prox-regular, subdifferentially continuous function, tilt stability is equivalent to uniform positive definiteness of the limiting second-order subdifferential at nearby attentive graph points.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and lower semicontinuous.
\(f\) is prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is tilt-stable}\iff\partial^2f\text{ is uniformly positive definite on nearby attentive graph points}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Generalized-Hessian Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional smooth specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is \(C^2\) near a stationary point \(\bar x\), then \(\bar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer if and only if \(\nabla^2f(\bar x)\) is positive definite. In that case the localized tilt response \(x(v)\) satisfies
\[
Dx(0)=\bigl(\nabla^2f(\bar x)\bigr)^{-1}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a smooth stationary point, tilt stability is exactly positive definiteness of the Hessian.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x\text{ is tilt-stable}\iff\nabla^2f(\bar x)\succ0.\)

assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, prox-regular, and subdifferentially continuous at \((\bar x,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tilt stability is equivalent to local strong metric regularity of \(\partial f\), and admits a positive-definite second-order subdifferential characterization.

For sufficiently small \(\gamma>0\), define
\[
M_\gamma(v)=\mathop{\operatorname{argmin}}_{\lVert x-\bar x\rVert\le\gamma}\{f(x)-\langle v,x\rangle\}.

The point \(\bar x\) is a tilt-stable local minimizer precisely when \(M_\gamma\) is single-valued and Lipschitz near \(0\), with \(M_\gamma(0)=\bar x\); equivalently, \(\partial f\) is strongly metrically regular at \((\bar x,0)\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graphically hemi-Lipschitzian, graphically Lipschitzian, graphically hemismooth, and graphically smooth mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local graph-representation classes for multifunctions between Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) and \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\). The mapping \(F\) is graphically hemi-Lipschitzian around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist a Banach space \(Z=X_1\times Y_1\), a mapping \(g:X\times Y\to Z\) strictly differentiable at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with surjective derivative, neighborhoods \(O\) of \((\bar x,\bar y)\) and \(O_1\) of \(\bar z=g(\bar x,\bar y)\), and a locally Lipschitz mapping \(f:X_1\to Y_1\) such that \((\operatorname{gph}F)\cap O=g^{-1}((\operatorname{gph}f)\cap O_1)\). It is graphically Lipschitzian if, additionally, \(\nabla g(\bar x,\bar y)\) is invertible. It is graphically hemismooth at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if it is graphically hemi-Lipschitzian there and \(f\) can be chosen strictly differentiable at \(\bar u\in X_1\) with \((\bar u,f(\bar u))=\bar z\). It is graphically smooth if, additionally, \(\nabla g(\bar x,\bar y)\) is invertible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These four classes describe graphs that locally become graphs of single-valued Lipschitz or strictly differentiable mappings under a strictly differentiable transformation. Surjectivity gives the hemi-classes, while invertibility gives the corresponding graphical Lipschitz or smooth classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ belongs to the respective graphical class exactly under the stated representation, differentiability, and derivative conditions.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes strict continuity through bounded truncations and establishes uniform Lipschitz estimates for graph-convex mappings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m$ be closed-valued, let $X\subset\operatorname{dom}S$, set $\rho_0:=\sup_{x\in X}d(0,S(x))$, and define $S_\rho(x):=S(x)\cap\rho\mathbb B$. (a) If $S$ is convex-valued, $\rho_0<\infty$, and $\bar\rho>\rho_0$, then $S$ is strictly continuous relative to $X$ if and only if, for every $\rho>2\bar\rho$, $S_\rho$ is locally Lipschitz continuous relative to $X$. (b) If $S$ is graph-convex and $X$ is compact with $X\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}S)$, then $\rho_0<\infty$ and there exists $\lambda\ge0$ such that, for every $\rho\ge\rho_0+1$, $S_\rho(x')\subset S_\rho(x)+\lambda\rho|x'-x|\mathbb B$ for all $x\in X$ and $x'\in\mathbb R^n$. Hence $\widehat d_\rho(S(x'),S(x))\le\lambda\rho|x'-x|$ for all $x,x'\in X$. One may take $\lambda=2/\inf\{d(x,X)\mid d(0,S(x))\ge\rho_0+1\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed-valued convex-valued mapping whose values remain uniformly within finite distance of zero on the reference set, strict continuity relative to that set is equivalent to local Lipschitz continuity of every sufficiently large bounded truncation. If the graph is convex and the reference set is compact and contained in the domain interior, the truncations satisfy a uniform Lipschitz inclusion and the associated truncated-distance estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[S\text{ is strictly continuous relative to }X\bigr]\iff\bigl[\forall\rho>2\bar\rho,\ S_\rho\text{ is locally Lipschitz continuous relative to }X\bigr];\quad \text{under (b), }\exists\lambda\ge0\ \forall\rho\ge\rho_0+1:\ S_\rho(x')\subset S_\rho(x)+\lambda\rho|x'-x|\mathbb B.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graphical Lipschitz Geometry of Prox-Regular Subgradient Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes an n-dimensional graphical Lipschitz property under prox-regularity and subdifferential continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous at \bar x for \bar v\in\partial f(\bar x). Then \partial f:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n is graphically Lipschitzian of dimension n around (\bar x,\bar v). Without subdifferential continuity, the same property holds for any sufficiently close f-attentive localization of \partial f around (\bar x,\bar v).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prox-regular and subdifferentially continuous function has a subgradient mapping whose graph is locally Lipschitzian of dimension n. Without subdifferential continuity, the conclusion applies to any sufficiently close attentive localization.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is prox-regular at }\bar x\text{ for }\bar v
f\text{ is subdifferentially continuous at }\bar x\text{ for }\bar v\text{, unless an }f\text{-attentive localization is used}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial f\text{ is graphically Lipschitzian of dimension }n\text{ around }(\bar x,\bar v);\text{ without subdifferential continuity, this holds for any sufficiently close }f\text{-attentive localization.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity of gradients on differentiability points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes strict differentiability and relative gradient continuity for regular functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let O\subset\mathbb{R}^n be open and let f be regular on O. At every x\in O where f is differentiable, f is strictly differentiable. If D=\{x\in O\mid f\text{ is differentiable at }x\}, then \nabla f:D\to\mathbb{R}^n is continuous relative to D. In particular, these conclusions hold when O is open and convex and f is finite and convex on O.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular function on an open set is strictly differentiable at each differentiability point, and its gradient is continuous relative to the set of such points. This applies in particular to finite convex functions on open convex sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in O,\ f\text{ differentiable at }x\Rightarrow f\text{ strictly differentiable at }x,\qquad \nabla f\big|_D\text{ is continuous},\quad D=\{x\in O:f\text{ is differentiable at }x\};\text{ in particular, this holds when }O\text{ is open convex and }f\text{ is finite convex on }O.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz versus sub-Lipschitz continuity under boundedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global implication and bounded-image equivalence, together with local equivalence to strict continuity under local boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\). Lipschitz continuity of \(S\) on \(X\) implies sub-Lipschitz continuity on \(X\). If \(S(X)\) is bounded, the two properties are equivalent. If \(S\) is locally bounded on \(X\), then local Lipschitz continuity, local sub-Lipschitz continuity, and strict continuity relative to \(X\) are equivalent. In particular, if \(S\) is strictly continuous and locally bounded relative to \(X\) at \(\bar x\), then it is Lipschitz continuous on a neighborhood of \(\bar x\) relative to \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lipschitz continuity always implies sub-Lipschitz continuity, and boundedness of the entire image makes the two properties equivalent. Under local boundedness, their local versions are also equivalent to strict continuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{Lip}_X(S)\Rightarrow\operatorname{subLip}_X(S);\quad S(X)\text{ bounded}\Rightarrow[\operatorname{Lip}_X(S)\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{subLip}_X(S)];\quad S\text{ locally bounded on }X\Rightarrow[\operatorname{locLip}_X(S)\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{locSubLip}_X(S)\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{StrictCont}_X(S)]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz-Like and Lipschitz Continuity of Multifunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines relative and local Lipschitz-like behavior, exact Lipschitz bounds, and Lipschitz continuity in Hausdorff distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) satisfy \(\operatorname{dom}F\ne\varnothing\), and let nonempty \(U\subset X\) and \(V\subset Y\) be given. The mapping \(F\) is Lipschitz-like on \(U\) relative to \(V\) with modulus \(\ell\ge0\) if
\[
F(x)\cap V\subset F(u)+\ell\|x-u\|\mathbb B\qquad\text{for all }x,u\in U.
\]
For \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), it is locally Lipschitz-like around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) with modulus \(\ell\) when the inclusion holds for neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\). The infimum of such moduli is \(\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y)\). This property is also called the Aubin or pseudo-Lipschitz property. Taking \(V=Y\) defines Lipschitz continuity on \(U\) and local Lipschitz continuity around \(\bar x\), with exact bound \(\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x)\). Moreover, Lipschitz continuity on \(U\) is equivalent to
\[
\operatorname{haus}(F(x),F(u))\le \ell\|x-u\|\qquad(x,u\in U),
\]
where
\[
\operatorname{haus}(\Omega_1,
0\Omega_2):=\inf\{\eta\ge0:\Omega_1\subset\Omega_2+
0\eta\mathbb B,\ \Omega_2\subset\Omega_1+
0\eta\mathbb B\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lipschitz-like behavior is a localized one-sided inclusion for multifunction values. Its graph-local form is the Aubin property, and the least admissible modulus is the exact Lipschitz bound. Removing image localization gives multifunction Lipschitz continuity, equivalently a Lipschitz estimate in Hausdorff distance.
assumptions_latex: U\subset X\text{ and }V\subset Y\text{ are nonempty}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F(x)\cap V\subset F(u)+\ell\|x-u\|\mathbb B\quad(x,u\in U);\qquad V=Y\Longleftrightarrow \operatorname{haus}(F(x),F(u))\le\ell\|x-u\|

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes strict continuity of closed-valued graph-convex mappings at interior domain points and bounds the truncated local Lipschitz modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If $S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m$ is closed-valued and graph-convex, then $S$ is strictly continuous at every $\bar x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}S)$. Moreover, for every $\rho>d(0,S(\bar x))+1$, one has $\widehat{\operatorname{lip}}_\rho S(\bar x)\le 2\rho/\bar\eta$, where $\bar\eta$ is the positive distance from $\bar x$ to $\{x\mid d(0,S(x))\ge d(0,S(\bar x))+1\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every closed-valued graph-convex set-valued mapping is strictly continuous at each interior point of its domain. For any sufficiently large truncation radius, its truncated local Lipschitz modulus is bounded by twice that radius divided by the specified positive separation distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is strictly continuous at }\bar x,\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{lip}}_\rho S(\bar x)\le\frac{2\rho}{\bar\eta}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inverse correspondence between Lipschitzian and metric regularity properties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative and exact-bound correspondences for a multifunction and its inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) with \(\operatorname{dom}F\ne\varnothing\). For \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), \(F\) is locally Lipschitz-like around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if \(F^{-1}\) is locally metrically regular around \((\bar y,\bar x)\), and \(\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y)=\operatorname{reg}F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)\). This is also equivalent to the existence of neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\), \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(\ell\ge 0\) such that \(F(x)\cap V\subset F(u)+\ell\lVert x-u\rVert\mathbb B\) for all \(u\in U\) and \(x\in X\). Furthermore, \(F\) is locally Lipschitzian around \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}F\) if and only if \(F^{-1}\) is semilocally metrically regular around \(\bar x\in\operatorname{rge}F^{-1}\), in which case \(\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x)=\operatorname{reg}F^{-1}(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local Lipschitz-like property of a multifunction is equivalent to local metric regularity of its inverse, with identical exact bounds. Local Lipschitzness is similarly equivalent to semilocal metric regularity of the inverse, again with equal bounds.
assumptions_latex: (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\text{ for the graph-point equivalence}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y)=\operatorname{reg}F^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x),\qquad \operatorname{lip}F(\bar x)=\operatorname{reg}F^{-1}(\bar x),\text{ together with the corresponding qualitative equivalences.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Lipschitz Continuity of Locally Compact Multifunctions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equates local Lipschitz continuity with pointwise Aubin properties under closedness and local compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be closed at \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}F\) and locally compact around \(\bar x\). Then \(F\) is locally Lipschitz around \(\bar x\) if and only if it is locally Lipschitz-like around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) for every \(\bar y\in F(\bar x)\). In this case,
\[
\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x)=\max\{\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y):\bar y\in F(\bar x)\}<\infty.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a multifunction is closed at and locally compact around a reference point, local Lipschitz continuity there is equivalent to the Aubin property at every value above that point. Its exact modulus is the finite maximum of the graph-point moduli.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is locally compact around }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is locally Lipschitz around }\bar x\iff (\forall\bar y\in F(\bar x))\ F\text{ is locally Lipschitz-like around }(\bar x,\bar y),\qquad \operatorname{lip}F(\bar x)=\max_{\bar y\in F(\bar x)}\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y)<\infty

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strictly and weak-star strictly Lipschitzian mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential refinements of local Lipschitz continuity for single-valued mappings between Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:X\to Y be Lipschitz continuous around \bar x and set y_k:=\frac{f(x_k+t_kv)-f(x_k)}{t_k}. The mapping f is strictly Lipschitzian at \bar x if there is a neighborhood V of 0 in X such that, whenever v\in V, x_k\to\bar x, and t_k\downarrow0, the sequence (y_k) contains a norm-convergent subsequence. It is w^*\text{-strictly Lipschitzian at }\bar x if there is a neighborhood V of 0 such that, for every v\in X and all x_k\to\bar x, t_k\downarrow0, and y_k^*\overset{w^*}{\to}0, one has \langle y_k^*,y_k\rangle\to0. If \dim Y<\infty, both properties hold for every locally Lipschitzian f.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict Lipschitzianity requires directional difference quotients, for directions near zero, to possess norm-convergent subsequences. Weak-star strict Lipschitzianity requires weak-star null dual sequences to pair to zero with the difference quotients under the source's stated quantifiers. For finite-dimensional ranges, both conditions reduce to local Lipschitz continuity.
assumptions_latex: f:X\to Y\text{ is a mapping between Banach spaces}
f\text{ is Lipschitz continuous around }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The stated sequential conditions define strict and }w^*\text{-strict Lipschitzianity at }\bar x;\quad \dim Y<\infty\Rightarrow\text{both reduce to local Lipschitz continuity}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The mapping \(F\) has the Aubin property at \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and a constant \(\kappa\ge0\), such that
\[
F(x_1)\cap V\subset F(x_2)+\kappa\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert\mathbb B_Y
\quad\text{for all }x_1,x_2\in U.
\]
Thus every value of \(F(x_1)\) near \(\bar y\) lies within \(\kappa\lVert x_1-x_2\rVert\) of some value of \(F(x_2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Aubin property bounds the movement of every nearby localized value by a constant times the change in the input.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the relative and unrestricted Aubin properties, their exact graphical modulus, and local stability along the graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\), \(\bar x\in X\), and \(\bar u\in S(\bar x)\), and suppose \(\operatorname{gph}S\) is locally closed at \((\bar x,\bar u)\). The mapping \(S\) has the Aubin property relative to \(X\) at \(\bar x\) for \(\bar u\) if there exist \(V\in\mathcal N(\bar x)\), \(W\in\mathcal N(\bar u)\), and \(\kappa\ge0\) such that \[S(x')\cap W\subset S(x)+\kappa\lVert x'-x\rVert\mathbb B\qquad\forall x,x'\in X\cap V.\] Replacing \(X\cap V\) by \(V\) gives the unrestricted Aubin property. Its graphical modulus is \[\operatorname{lip}S(\bar x\mid\bar u):=\inf\{\kappa\ge0:\text{the unrestricted inclusion holds for some }V,W\}.\] If the Aubin property holds at \((\bar x,\bar u)\), then it holds at all sufficiently nearby \((x,u)\in\operatorname{gph}S\), and \((x,u)\mapsto\operatorname{lip}S(x\mid u)\) is upper semicontinuous relative to the graph locally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Aubin property is a localized Lipschitz-like condition for a set-valued mapping near a selected graph point. Its graphical modulus is the infimum of the admissible constants. The property persists at nearby graph points, where the modulus is locally upper semicontinuous along the graph.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}S\text{ is locally closed at }(\bar x,\bar u)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S(x')\cap W\subset S(x)+\kappa\lVert x'-x\rVert\mathbb B\quad\forall x,x'\in X\cap V,\qquad \operatorname{lip}S(\bar x\mid\bar u)=\inf\kappa,\text{ with local stability and relative upper semicontinuity along }\operatorname{gph}S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Horizon-Subgradient Characterization of Epigraphical Aubin Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between a horizon-subgradient qualification and the Aubin property of a parameterized epigraph mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be proper and lsc, let (\bar x,\bar u)\in\operatorname{dom}f, and define E(u)=\operatorname{epi}f(\cdot,u). Then \big[(0,y)\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x,\bar u)\Rightarrow y=0\big] if and only if E has the Aubin property at \bar u for (\bar x,f(\bar x,\bar u)).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous parameterized function, the absence of a nonzero parameter component in any horizon subgradient having zero decision-variable component is equivalent to the Aubin property of the parameterized epigraph mapping at the specified graph point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \big[(0,y)\in\partial^\infty f(\bar x,\bar u)\Rightarrow y=0\big]\iff E\text{ has the Aubin property at }\bar u\text{ for }(\bar x,f(\bar x,\bar u)).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Preservation of the Aubin Property under Composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Composition rule for Lipschitz-like set-valued mappings and a conditional product bound for the exact modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G:X\rightrightarrows Y and F:Y\rightrightarrows Z be set-valued mappings between Asplund spaces, and let \bar z\in(F\circ G)(\bar x). Assume that the graphs of G and F^{-1} are locally closed near \bar x and \bar z, respectively; that (x,z)\mapsto G(x)\cap F^{-1}(z) is inner semicompact around (\bar x,\bar z); and that, for every \bar y\in G(\bar x)\cap F^{-1}(\bar z), G is Lipschitz-like around (\bar x,\bar y) and F is Lipschitz-like around (\bar y,\bar z). Then F\circ G is Lipschitz-like around (\bar x,\bar z). If additionally \dim X<\infty and, for every such \bar y, G and F are coderivatively normal at (\bar x,\bar y) and (\bar y,\bar z), respectively, then \operatorname{lip}(F\circ G)(\bar x,\bar z)\leq\sup_{\bar y\in G(\bar x)\cap F^{-1}(\bar z)}\operatorname{lip}G(\bar x,\bar y)\operatorname{lip}F(\bar y,\bar z).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local closedness, inner semicompactness of the intermediate-value mapping, and the Aubin property of both factors at every relevant intermediate value imply the Aubin property of their composition. A supremum-of-products bound for the exact modulus additionally requires a finite-dimensional domain and coderivative normality of both factors at all relevant points.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}G\text{ and }\operatorname{gph}F^{-1}\text{ are locally closed as stated}
(x,z)\mapsto G(x)\cap F^{-1}(z)\text{ is inner semicompact around }(\bar x,\bar z)
\forall\bar y\in G(\bar x)\cap F^{-1}(\bar z),\;G\text{ and }F\text{ have the Aubin property at the corresponding graph points}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\circ G\text{ is Lipschitz-like around }(\bar x,\bar z);\quad \dim X<\infty\text{ and pointwise coderivative normality}\Rightarrow\operatorname{lip}(F\circ G)\leq\sup_{\bar y}\operatorname{lip}G\,\operatorname{lip}F.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended Formulation of the Aubin Property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes an equivalent defining inclusion in which one argument ranges over the entire reference set, without changing the unrestricted graphical modulus.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^m\), let \((\bar x,\bar u)\in\operatorname{gph}S\) with \(\operatorname{gph}S\) locally closed at that point, let \(X\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) contain \(\bar x\), and let \(\kappa\ge0\). The following are equivalent: \[(a)\quad \exists V\in\mathcal N(\bar x),\ W\in\mathcal N(\bar u):\ S(x')\cap W\subset S(x)+\kappa\lVert x'-x\rVert\mathbb B\quad\forall x,x'\in X\cap V;\] \[(b)\quad \exists V\in\mathcal N(\bar x),\ W\in\mathcal N(\bar u):\ S(x')\cap W\subset S(x)+\kappa\lVert x'-x\rVert\mathbb B\quad\forall x\in X\cap V,\ \forall x'\in X.\] Hence (b) may replace (a) in the relative Aubin definition. When \(X\) is suppressed, the infimum of the constants valid in (b) is still \(\operatorname{lip}S(\bar x\mid\bar u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The usual local two-point inclusion for the relative Aubin property is equivalent to a formulation where the first point remains local and the second may range over the whole reference set. In the unrestricted case, the extended formulation gives the same graphical modulus.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{gph}S\text{ is locally closed at }(\bar x,\bar u)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\iff(b),\qquad \inf\{\kappa:\text{the unrestricted extended inclusion holds}\}=\operatorname{lip}S(\bar x\mid\bar u).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The Aubin property specialized to the parameterized epigraph mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \((\bar x,\bar v)\in\operatorname{dom}L\). The function \(L\) is locally epi-Lipschitz near \((\bar x,\bar v)\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\), \(V\), and \(W\) of \(\bar x\), \(\bar v\), and \(L(\bar x,\bar v)\), respectively, and \(k>0\) such that, for all \(x',x''\in U\), \[\operatorname{epi}L(x',\cdot)\cap(V\times W)\subseteq \operatorname{epi}L(x'',\cdot)+k\lvert x'-x''\rvert B.\] This is also called the Aubin continuity property; when \(L(x,\cdot)\) is an indicator function, it is called the pseudo-Lipschitz property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local epi-Lipschitz continuity bounds the change of localized epigraphs proportionally to the change in the parameter. It is the Aubin property of the epigraph mapping and is called pseudo-Lipschitz continuity for indicator functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists U,V,W,\ k>0\ \forall x',x''\in U:\ \operatorname{epi}L(x',\cdot)\cap(V\times W)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}L(x'',\cdot)+k\lvert x'-x''\rvert B

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aubin-property criteria and exact modulus for regular constraint systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coderivative criteria and exact Lipschitz-modulus formulas for constraint-system solution maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F(x):=\{y\mid g(x,y)\in\Theta,\ (x,y)\in\Omega\} between Asplund spaces, let (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F, and set \bar z=g(\bar x,\bar y), where \Theta is locally closed and SNC at \bar z. (i) If Z is Banach, \Omega=X\times Y, and g is strictly differentiable at (\bar x,\bar y) with surjective derivative, then (x^*,0)\in\nabla g(\bar x,\bar y)^*N(\bar z;\Theta)\Rightarrow x^*=0 is sufficient for the Aubin property of F. It is also necessary when F is strongly coderivatively normal, in particular when \dim Y<\infty. If \dim X<\infty, then \operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y)=\sup\{\|x^*\|\mid(x^*,-y^*)\in\nabla g(\bar x,\bar y)^*N(\bar z;\Theta),\ \|y^*\|\le1\}; the supremum is attained if \operatorname{gph}N(\cdot;\Theta) is locally closed near \bar z in the norm\times weak^* topology. (ii) Suppose Z is Asplund, \Theta is normally regular at \bar z, \Omega is locally closed, normally regular, and PSNC with respect to X at (\bar x,\bar y), g is strictly differentiable there or is N-regular there with \dim Z<\infty, and (D_N^*g\circ N(\bar z;\Theta))\cap[-N((\bar x,\bar y);\Omega)]=\{0\} and N(\bar z;\Theta)\cap\ker D_N^*g=\{0\}. Then, for the corresponding coderivative D^*, (x^*,0)\in D^*g(\bar x,\bar y)\circ N(\bar z;\Theta)+N((\bar x,\bar y);\Omega)\Rightarrow x^*=0 is necessary and sufficient for the Aubin property. If \dim X<\infty, \operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y) equals the supremum of \|x^*\| over the same coderivative-normal sum subject to \|y^*\|\le1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For regular constraint systems, exclusion of nonzero parameter-dual coderivative elements with zero output-dual component characterizes the Aubin property under the stated normality assumptions. In finite-dimensional parameter spaces, the exact Lipschitz modulus is the corresponding coderivative norm supremum.
assumptions_latex: F(x)=\{y\mid g(x,y)\in\Theta,\ (x,y)\in\Omega\},\quad \bar z=g(\bar x,\bar y),\quad \Theta\text{ locally closed and SNC at }\bar z
\text{Case (i): }Z\text{ Banach},\ \Omega=X\times Y,\ g\text{ strictly differentiable with surjective derivative}
\text{Case (ii): }Z\text{ Asplund},\ \Theta\text{ normally regular},\ \Omega\text{ locally closed, normally regular, and PSNC with respect to }X
g\text{ is strictly differentiable or is N-regular with }\dim Z<\infty
(D_N^*g\circ N(\bar z;\Theta))\cap[-N((\bar x,\bar y);\Omega)]=\{0\},\quad N(\bar z;\Theta)\cap\ker D_N^*g=\{0\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ has the Aubin property exactly under the stated zero-output coderivative implication whenever necessity is asserted; if }\dim X<\infty,\ \operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y)\text{ equals the stated supremum}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aubin property of the inverse of a strictly differentiable mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Surjective-derivative criterion and exact Lipschitz modulus for the set-valued inverse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:X\to Y$ be strictly differentiable at $\bar x$, and let $\bar y=f(\bar x)$. Then $f^{-1}:Y\rightrightarrows X$ is locally Lipschitz-like around $(\bar y,\bar x)$ if and only if $\nabla f(\bar x)$ is surjective. In that case, $$\operatorname{lip}f^{-1}(\bar y,\bar x)=\left\|\big(\nabla f(\bar x)^*\big)^{-1}\right\|.$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inverse of a strictly differentiable mapping has the Aubin property at the reference graph point exactly when the derivative is surjective, and its exact Lipschitz modulus is the norm of the inverse adjoint.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aubin Property of a Set-Valued Mapping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local Lipschitz-like, or pseudo-Lipschitz, behavior around a graph point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mapping \(\Gamma:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\) has the Aubin property at \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}\Gamma\) if there exist neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(V\) of \(\bar y\), and \(L_\Gamma<\infty\), such that for every \(x,x'\in U\) and \(y\in\Gamma(x)\cap V\), there exists \(y'\in\Gamma(x')\) with \(\|y-y'\|\le L_\Gamma\|x-x'\|\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{dist}(y,\Gamma(x'))\le L_\Gamma\|x-x'\|\) for all such \(x,x',y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Aubin, Lipschitz-like, or pseudo-Lipschitz property requires every nearby graph value to be approximable by a value at another nearby parameter, with error bounded linearly by the parameter displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists U,V,L_\Gamma<\infty\ \forall x,x'\in U\ \forall y\in\Gamma(x)\cap V:\ \operatorname{dist}(y,\Gamma(x'))\le L_\Gamma\|x-x'\|.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Neighborhood coderivative characterization of the Aubin property
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the Lipschitz-like property of a locally closed-graph multifunction between Asplund spaces and computes its exact Lipschitz modulus using nearby regular coderivative norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\rightrightarrows Y\) be a set-valued mapping between Asplund spaces, let \((\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F\), and assume that \(F\) is closed-graph around \((\bar x,\bar y)\). Then \(F\) is Lipschitz-like around \((\bar x,\bar y)\) if and only if there exist \(\ell>0\) and \(\eta>0\) such that, whenever \(x\in B_\eta(\bar x)\), \(y\in F(x)\cap B_\eta(\bar y)\), and \(y^*\in Y^*\), \[\sup\{\|x^*\|\mid x^*\in\widehat D^*F(x,y)(y^*)\}\leq \ell\|y^*\|.\] Moreover, \[\operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y)=\inf_{\eta>0}\sup\{\|\widehat D^*F(x,y)\|\mid x\in B_\eta(\bar x),\ y\in F(x)\cap B_\eta(\bar y)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a set-valued mapping between Asplund spaces whose graph is locally closed around the reference graph point, the Aubin property is equivalent to a uniform neighborhood bound on the regular coderivative. Its exact Lipschitz modulus is the infimum over neighborhood radii of the supremum of the corresponding nearby regular-coderivative norms.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is closed-graph around }(\bar x,\bar y)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is Lipschitz-like around }(\bar x,\bar y)\iff \exists\ell,\eta>0\ \forall x\in B_\eta(\bar x),\ \forall y\in F(x)\cap B_\eta(\bar y),\ \forall y^*\in Y^*:\ \sup\{\|x^*\|\mid x^*\in\widehat D^*F(x,y)(y^*)\}\leq\ell\|y^*\|,\quad \operatorname{lip}F(\bar x,\bar y)=\inf_{\eta>0}\sup_{\substack{x\in B_\eta(\bar x)\\y\in F(x)\cap B_\eta(\bar y)}}\|\widehat D^*F(x,y)\|.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Aubin and strict-continuity calculus under composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of Lipschitz-like and strict continuity properties under composition of outer-semicontinuous multifunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let S=S_2\circ S_1, where S_1:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^p and S_2:\mathbb R^p\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m are outer semicontinuous. Let \bar x\in\operatorname{dom}S and \bar u\in S(\bar x), and suppose (x,u)\mapsto S_1(x)\cap S_2^{-1}(u) is locally bounded at (\bar x,\bar u). If S_1 has the Aubin property at \bar x for every \bar w\in S_1(\bar x)\cap S_2^{-1}(\bar u), and S_2 has the Aubin property at each such \bar w for \bar u, then S has the Aubin property at \bar x for \bar u and
\operatorname{lip}S(\bar x\mid\bar u)\leq\max_{\bar w\in S_1(\bar x)\cap S_2^{-1}(\bar u)}\operatorname{lip}S_1(\bar x\mid\bar w)\operatorname{lip}S_2(\bar w\mid\bar u).
If S_1 and S_2 are graph-convex, the maximum can be replaced by the minimum. If S_1 is strictly continuous at \bar x, S_2 is strictly continuous at every point of S_1(\bar x), and the boundedness condition holds for every \bar u\in S(\bar x), then S is strictly continuous at \bar x. Separately, if S_1 is strictly continuous and locally bounded at \bar x and S_2 has both properties at every \bar w\in S_1(\bar x), then S is strictly continuous and locally bounded at \bar x, with
\operatorname{lip}_{\infty}S(\bar x)\leq\operatorname{lip}_{\infty}S_1(\bar x)\max_{\bar w\in S_1(\bar x)}\operatorname{lip}_{\infty}S_2(\bar w).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under local boundedness of feasible intermediate points, a composition inherits the Aubin property from both component mappings, with a maximum-product modulus bound and a minimum-product refinement in the graph-convex case. The stated pointwise or locally bounded strict-continuity hypotheses also yield strict continuity, local boundedness, and a uniform-modulus product bound.
assumptions_latex: S=S_2\circ S_1,\quad S_1:\mathbb R^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^p,\quad S_2:\mathbb R^p\rightrightarrows\mathbb R^m\text{ are outer semicontinuous}
(x,u)\mapsto S_1(x)\cap S_2^{-1}(u)\text{ is locally bounded at }(\bar x,\bar u)
S_1\text{ has the Aubin property at }\bar x\text{ for }\bar w\text{ and }S_2\text{ has it at }\bar w\text{ for }\bar u\quad\forall\bar w\in S_1(\bar x)\cap S_2^{-1}(\bar u)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ has the Aubin property at }\bar x\text{ for }\bar u,\quad \operatorname{lip}S(\bar x\mid\bar u)\leq\max_{\bar w}\operatorname{lip}S_1(\bar x\mid\bar w)\operatorname{lip}S_2(\bar w\mid\bar u),\text{ with the stated graph-convex and strict-continuity refinements.}
